Use \(\cos^2t=\frac{1+\cos2t}2\): the integrand is \(\frac32-2\cos t+\frac12\cos2t\), with antiderivative \(\frac32t-2\sin t+\frac14\sin2t\). At \(2\pi\) this is \(3\pi\) and at \(0\) it is \(0\). So \(A=3\pi a^2\), three times the area \(\pi a^2\) of the wheel. (b) The upper half is traced for \(0\le t\le\pi\), where \(y=3\sin t\ge0\) and \(f=5\cos t\) is decreasing (\(f'=-5\sin t\le0\)). By the decreasing case of Theorem 12.1.21,

\[\text{upper half}=-\int_0^\pi3\sin t\,(-5\sin t)\,dt=15\int_0^\pi\sin^2t\,dt=15\int_0^\pi\frac{1-\cos2t}2\,dt=15\cdot\frac\pi2.\]

By symmetry the whole area is twice this: \(A=15\pi\), which is \(\pi ab\) with \(a=5\), \(b=3\).

items.title: Surface area of a surface of revolution
items.text:
Revolve the curve \(C\) about the \(x\)-axis (\(g\ge0\)). Each chord of an inscribed polygon sweeps out the lateral surface of a frustum of a cone (or a cylinder, or a cone), and we define the area of the surface of revolution as the limit of the total area of these frusta as the mesh tends to \(0\).

Theorem 12.1.23: Lateral area of a frustum

A frustum of a right circular cone with end radii \(r_1,r_2\ge0\) and slant height \(\ell\) has lateral area \(\pi(r_1+r_2)\ell\).

Proof. A cone with base radius \(r\) and slant height \(s\), cut along a slant line and unrolled, is a circular sector of radius \(s\) and arc length \(2\pi r\); its area is \(\frac12s\cdot2\pi r=\pi rs\). If \(r_1=r_2\) the frustum is a cylinder, which unrolls to a rectangle \(2\pi r\times\ell\) of area \(2\pi r\ell\), as claimed. Otherwise let \(r_1<r_2\). Extend the frustum to a full cone of base radius \(r_2\) and slant height \(\ell+s_0\), from which a cone of base radius \(r_1\) and slant height \(s_0\) has been removed. By similar triangles \(\frac{s_0}{r_1}=\frac{\ell+s_0}{r_2}\), that is \(r_2s_0=r_1\ell+r_1s_0\), so \((r_2-r_1)s_0=r_1\ell\). The lateral area of the frustum is

\[\pi r_2(\ell+s_0)-\pi r_1s_0=\pi r_2\ell+\pi(r_2-r_1)s_0=\pi r_2\ell+\pi r_1\ell=\pi(r_1+r_2)\ell.\]

◻ ∎

Theorem 12.1.24: Surface area of a surface of revolution

Let \(f'\) and \(g'\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(g\ge0\). The area of the surface obtained by revolving \(C\) about the \(x\)-axis is

\[S=\int_a^b2\pi\,g(t)\sqrt{f'(t)^2+g'(t)^2}\,dt.\]

If \(f\ge0\), revolving \(C\) about the \(y\)-axis gives \(S=\int_a^b2\pi\,f(t)\sqrt{f'(t)^2+g'(t)^2}\,dt\).

Proof. The \(k\)th chord joins points at distances \(g(t_{k-1})\) and \(g(t_k)\) from the \(x\)-axis and has length \(\Delta_k\), so it sweeps out a frustum with \(r_1=g(t_{k-1})\), \(r_2=g(t_k)\) and \(\ell=\Delta_k\). By Theorem 12.1.23 the total area is

\[\sum_{k=1}^n\pi\bigl(g(t_{k-1})+g(t_k)\bigr)\Delta_k=\pi\sum g(t_{k-1})\Delta_k+\pi\sum g(t_k)\Delta_k.\]

Apply Theorem 12.1.18 with \(h=g\) twice, with \(\tau_k=t_{k-1}\) and with \(\tau_k=t_k\). Each sum tends to \(\int_a^bg\abs v\,dt\), so the total area tends to \(\pi\left(\int_a^bg\abs v\,dt+\int_a^bg\abs v\,dt\right)=2\pi\int_a^bg\abs v\,dt\). For the \(y\)-axis, the distances are \(f(t_{k-1})\) and \(f(t_k)\) and the same argument applies with \(h=f\). ◻ ∎

Example 12.1.25: Two surfaces

Find the area of the surface obtained by revolving about the \(x\)-axis (a) \(x=t^2\), \(y=2t\), \(0\le t\le1\); (b) the semicircle \(x=a\cos t\), \(y=a\sin t\), \(0\le t\le\pi\).

Solution. (a) The curve is the arc of the parabola \(y^2=4x\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,2)\). Here \(f'=2t\), \(g'=2\), so \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2}=\sqrt{4t^2+4}=2\sqrt{t^2+1}\) and \(g=2t\ge0\). By Theorem 12.1.24,

\[S=\int_0^12\pi(2t)\cdot2\sqrt{t^2+1}\,dt=8\pi\int_0^1t\sqrt{t^2+1}\,dt.\]

With \(u=t^2+1\), \(du=2t\,dt\): \(\int_0^1t\sqrt{t^2+1}\,dt=\frac12\int_1^2\sqrt u\,du=\frac12\cdot\frac23u^{3/2}\Big|_1^2=\frac{2\sqrt2-1}3\). So \(S=\frac{8\pi}3\left(2\sqrt2-1\right)\approx15.32\). Check. The straight segment from \((0,0)\) to \((1,2)\) generates a cone of radius \(2\) and slant height \(\sqrt5\), with lateral area \(\pi\cdot2\cdot\sqrt5\approx14.05\), a little smaller, as expected for a curve that bulges outward. (b) \(f'=-a\sin t\), \(g'=a\cos t\), so \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2}=a\) (for \(a>0\)), and \(g=a\sin t\ge0\) on \([0,\pi]\):

\[S=\int_0^\pi2\pi\,a\sin t\cdot a\,dt=2\pi a^2\bigl[-\cos t\bigr]_0^\pi=2\pi a^2(1+1)=4\pi a^2,\]

the area of a sphere of radius \(a\).

Looking ahead. Everything in this section extends to curves in space: a point \((x(t),y(t),z(t))\) or a vector-valued function, whose derivative is the velocity vector \(v(t)\) used above, with length \(\abs{v(t)}\) the speed. The arc length formula \(\int\abs{v}\,dt\) will carry over without change. The next section introduces another way to describe plane curves, polar coordinates, and a later chapter adds cylindrical and spherical coordinates for space. In a differential equations course a parametric curve is the usual picture of a solution of a system, and in physics it is the trajectory of a moving body.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Twenty further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Eliminating the parameter (Examples 12.1.26–12.1.28): a square root; a curve traced back and forth; a rational parametrization of the circle.

  2. Parametrizing curves (Examples 12.1.29–12.1.31): an ellipse with a given start; a segment with a time limit; the curve \(y^2=x^3\).

  3. Orientation, speed and repeated tracing (Examples 12.1.32–12.1.33): a circle traced three times; which descriptions give the same curve.

  4. Tangent lines and concavity (Examples 12.1.34–12.1.36): horizontal, vertical and ordinary tangents of a cubic; the tangents at a self-crossing; an inflection point.

  5. Arc length (Examples 12.1.37–12.1.39): an arc of a circle; a polynomial curve with a perfect square; an infinite spiral of finite length.

  6. Area and surface area (Examples 12.1.40–12.1.42): an area; a cone checked by geometry; the torus.

  7. Proofs (Examples 12.1.43–12.1.45).

items.title: Group 1: Eliminating the parameter
items.text:
Example 12.1.26: A square root in the parameter

Eliminate \(t\) from \(x=\sqrt t+1\), \(y=2t-1\), \(t\ge0\), and describe the curve and its orientation.

Solution. Isolate the square root: \(\sqrt t=x-1\). Since \(\sqrt t\ge0\), we need \(x\ge1\), and squaring gives \(t=(x-1)^2\). Substitute into \(y=2t-1\):

\[y=2(x-1)^2-1=2x^2-4x+2-1=2x^2-4x+1,\qquad x\ge1.\]

As \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(\infty\), \(x=\sqrt t+1\) increases from \(1\) to \(\infty\), so the curve is the right half of the parabola \(y=2(x-1)^2-1\), starting at its vertex \((1,-1)\) (\(t=0\)) and traced from left to right. Check. \(t=4\) gives \((3,7)\), and \(2(3-1)^2-1=7\).

Example 12.1.27: A curve traced back and forth

Describe \(x=2\sin t\), \(y=1-\cos2t\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\), by eliminating the parameter and by following the motion.

Solution. The double-angle identity \(\cos2t=1-2\sin^2t\) gives \(y=1-(1-2\sin^2t)=2\sin^2t\). Since \(\sin t=\frac x2\), \(y=2\left(\frac x2\right)^2=\frac{x^2}2\). As \(x=2\sin t\) takes every value in \([-2,2]\), the points lie on the arc \(y=\frac{x^2}2\), \(-2\le x\le2\) (heights \(0\) to \(2\)). To see how it is traced, tabulate:

\[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t&0&\frac\pi2&\pi&\frac{3\pi}2&2\pi\\\hline (x,y)&(0,0)&(2,2)&(0,0)&(-2,2)&(0,0) \end{array}\]

The point goes up the right half to \((2,2)\), back down to the origin, up the left half to \((-2,2)\) and back to the origin: each half is traced twice (up and down). The curve is not traced once from left to right; the orientation changes every quarter period.

Example 12.1.28: A rational parametrization of the circle

Show that \(x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\), \(y=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}\), \(-\infty<t<\infty\), traces the unit circle with exactly one point missing, and find the orientation.

Solution. On the circle. \(x^2+y^2=\dfrac{(1-t^2)^2+4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=\dfrac{1-2t^2+t^4+4t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=\dfrac{1+2t^2+t^4}{(1+t^2)^2}=1\). The missing point. \(x=-1\) would need \(1-t^2=-(1+t^2)\), that is \(1=-1\), which is impossible; so \((-1,0)\) is never reached. Every other point is reached. Let \((x,y)\) be on the circle with \(x\ne-1\) and put \(t=\frac y{1+x}\). From \(y^2=1-x^2=(1-x)(1+x)\) we get \(t^2=\frac{y^2}{(1+x)^2}=\frac{1-x}{1+x}\). Then \(1+t^2=\frac2{1+x}\) and \(1-t^2=\frac{2x}{1+x}\), so \(\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}=x\) and \(\frac{2t}{1+t^2}=2\cdot\frac y{1+x}\cdot\frac{1+x}2=y\). Orientation. \(t=-1,0,1\) give \((0,-1)\), \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\): counterclockwise. As \(t\to\pm\infty\) the point approaches \((-1,0)\) (the missing point).

items.title: Group 2: Parametrizing curves
items.text:
Example 12.1.29: An ellipse that starts at the top

Find parametric equations for the ellipse with center \((1,-2)\), horizontal semi-axis \(3\) and vertical semi-axis \(5\), traced counterclockwise once from its top point.

Solution. The top point is \((1,-2+5)=(1,3)\). Try \(x=1-3\sin t\), \(y=-2+5\cos t\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\). At \(t=0\) this is \((1,3)\). The velocity at \(t=0\) is \((-3\cos0,\,-5\sin0)=(-3,0)\): the point moves left at the top, which is counterclockwise. The points are on the ellipse because

\[\left(\frac{x-1}3\right)^2+\left(\frac{y+2}5\right)^2=\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1.\]

Check the quarter points. \(t=\frac\pi2\): \((1-3,\,-2)=(-2,-2)\) (left); \(t=\pi\): \((1,-7)\) (bottom); \(t=\frac{3\pi}2\): \((4,-2)\) (right). Top, left, bottom, right is counterclockwise, and \(t=2\pi\) returns to \((1,3)\).

Example 12.1.30: A segment traversed in a given time

A drone flies in a straight line from \(P(-2,5)\) to \(Q(4,-1)\) at constant velocity, taking \(3\) seconds. Find its position at time \(t\), the point where it crosses the \(y\)-axis, and its speed.

Solution. By Theorem 12.1.7(2) with \(s=\frac t3\): \(x=-2+6\cdot\frac t3=-2+2t\), \(y=5-6\cdot\frac t3=5-2t\), \(0\le t\le3\). Check. \(t=3\) gives \((4,-1)=Q\). The \(y\)-axis is where \(x=0\): \(-2+2t=0\), \(t=1\), at the point \((0,3)\). The velocity is \((2,-2)\) and the speed is \(\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2\) (the arc length integrand of Theorem 12.1.19). Over \(3\) seconds the distance flown is \(3\cdot2\sqrt2=6\sqrt2\), which equals the distance \(\sqrt{6^2+6^2}=6\sqrt2\) from \(P\) to \(Q\).

Example 12.1.31: The curve \(y^2=x^3\)

Show that \(x=t^2\), \(y=t^3\), \(-\infty<t<\infty\), describes the complete curve \(y^2=x^3\), and find the tangent at the origin.

Solution. Contained in the curve. \(y^2=t^6=(t^2)^3=x^3\). Every point is reached. Let \(y^2=x^3\). Then \(x\ge0\) (a square is nonnegative), and if \(x>0\) put \(t=\frac yx\). Then \(t^2=\frac{y^2}{x^2}=\frac{x^3}{x^2}=x\) and \(t^3=\frac{y^3}{x^3}=\frac{y\cdot y^2}{x^3}=y\). If \(x=0\) then \(y=0\), the point \(t=0\). Tangent at the origin. \(f'(0)=0\) and \(g'(0)=0\) (at \(t=0\): \(2t=0\) and \(3t^2=0\)), so Theorem 12.1.12 does not apply; take the limit: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2}{2t}=\frac{3t}2\to0\) as \(t\to0\). The curve arrives at the origin with a horizontal tangent from both sides (\(y=\pm x^{3/2}\)) and turns back: a cusp.

items.title: Group 3: Orientation, speed and repeated tracing
items.text:
Example 12.1.32: A circle traced three times

Describe \(x=2\cos3t\), \(y=2\sin3t\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\): the curve, the orientation, the number of laps and the arc length given by the formula.

Solution. \(x^2+y^2=4\left(\cos^23t+\sin^23t\right)=4\): a circle of radius \(2\) about the origin, counterclockwise because \(\omega=3>0\) (Theorem 12.1.4). One lap takes \(\frac{2\pi}3\), so the interval \([0,2\pi]\) holds \(\frac{2\pi}{2\pi/3}=3\) laps. The speed is \(\sqrt{(-6\sin3t)^2+(6\cos3t)^2}=6\), so the formula gives \(L=\int_0^{2\pi}6\,dt=12\pi\), three times the circumference \(4\pi\) of the circle. It measures the distance travelled, not the length of the set of points (compare Pause and think 12.1.3).

Example 12.1.33: Same curve, or not?

Which of (a) \(x=t\), \(y=t^2\), \(-2\le t\le2\); (b) \(x=t^3\), \(y=t^6\), \(-1\le t\le1\); (c) \(x=2\sin t\), \(y=4\sin^2t\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\) describe the same set of points?

Solution. (a) eliminating \(t=x\) gives \(y=x^2\) with \(-2\le x\le2\) (the arc, traced once from left to right). (b) \(y=t^6=(t^3)^2=x^2\), and \(x=t^3\) runs over \([-1,1]\): the arc \(y=x^2\) with \(-1\le x\le1\) only, which is a part of (a), so (b) is a different curve (its endpoints are \((\pm1,1)\), those of (a) are \((\pm2,4)\)). (c) \(y=4\sin^2t=\left(2\sin t\right)^2=x^2\) and \(x=2\sin t\) takes every value in \([-2,2]\): the same set as (a). But (c) goes out and back, as in Example 12.1.27: from \((0,0)\) to \((2,4)\), back, to \((-2,4)\), back. So (a) and (c) describe the same set of points, with different orientation behavior, and (b) is a different set.

items.title: Group 4: Tangent lines and concavity
items.text:
Example 12.1.34: Horizontal, vertical and ordinary tangents

For the curve \(x=t^2+1\), \(y=t^3-3t\) find all points with a horizontal or a vertical tangent, and the tangent line at \(t=2\).

Solution. \(f'=2t\) and \(g'=3t^2-3=3(t-1)(t+1)\). Horizontal: \(g'=0\) at \(t=\pm1\), where \(f'=\pm2 e0\). The points: \(t=1\): \((2,\,1-3)=(2,-2)\); \(t=-1\): \((2,\,-1+3)=(2,2)\). Vertical: \(f'=0\) at \(t=0\), where \(g'=-3 e0\): the point \((1,0)\). At \(t=2\): the point is \((5,\,8-6)=(5,2)\) and the slope is \( rac{g'(2)}{f'(2)}= rac{9}{4}\), so the tangent line is \(y-2= rac94(x-5)\), i.e. \(y= rac94x- rac{37}4\).

Example 12.1.35: Tangent lines at a self-crossing

The curve of Example 12.1.34 crosses itself. Find the crossing point and the two tangent lines there.

Solution. A crossing needs two values \(t_1 e t_2\) with the same point. Since \(x=t^2+1\) is the same for \(\pm t\), try \(t_2=-t_1\): then \(y=t^3-3t=t(t^2-3)\) is odd in \(t\), so the two \(y\)-values are equal only if \(y=0\), that is \(t=\pm\sqrt3\) (\(t=0\) gives the single value). At \(t=\pm\sqrt3\): \(x=3+1=4\), \(y=0\). The crossing point is \((4,0)\). The slopes are \( rac{dy}{dx}= rac{3(t^2-1)}{2t}= rac{3\cdot2}{\pm2\sqrt3}=\pm\sqrt3\). The tangent lines at \((4,0)\) are \(y=\sqrt3\,(x-4)\) (for \(t=\sqrt3\)) and \(y=-\sqrt3\,(x-4)\) (for \(t=-\sqrt3\)). They make angles of \(\pm60^\circ\) with the \(x\)-axis.

The red lines are the two tangent lines at the crossing, \(y=\pm\sqrt3\,(x-4)\); the horizontal tangents are at \((2,\pm2)\) and the vertical tangent at \((1,0)\).

Example 12.1.36: An inflection point

For \(x=t^3+t\), \(y=t^2\) find \( rac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the intervals of concavity and the inflection points.

Solution. \(f'=3t^2+1>0\), \(g'=2t\), \(f''=6t\), \(g''=2\). So \( rac{dy}{dx}= rac{2t}{3t^2+1}\) and, by Theorem 12.1.15,

\[ rac{d^2y}{dx^2}= rac{(3t^2+1)\cdot2-2t\cdot6t}{(3t^2+1)^3}= rac{2-6t^2}{(3t^2+1)^3}.\]

The denominator is positive, so the sign is that of \(2-6t^2\): positive for \(\abs t< rac1{\sqrt3}\) (concave up), negative for \(\abs t> rac1{\sqrt3}\) (concave down), and the concavity changes at \(t=\pm rac1{\sqrt3}\). The inflection points: \(y= rac13\) and \(x=t(t^2+1)=\pm rac1{\sqrt3}\cdot rac43=\pm rac{4\sqrt3}9\approx\pm0.77\), i.e. \(\left(\pm rac{4\sqrt3}9, rac13 ight)\).

items.title: Group 5: Arc length
items.text:
Example 12.1.37: An arc of a circle

Find the length of \(x=8\cos t\), \(y=8\sin t\), \(0\le t\le\frac\pi3\).

Solution. \(f'=-8\sin t\), \(g'=8\cos t\), so \(f'^2+g'^2=64\left(\sin^2t+\cos^2t\right)=64\) and the speed is \(8\). Then \(L=\int_0^{\pi/3}8\,dt=\frac{8\pi}3\approx8.378\). This is the familiar \(r\theta\) with \(r=8\) and \(\theta=\frac\pi3\).

Example 12.1.38: A perfect square under the root

Find the length of \(x=t-\frac{t^3}3\), \(y=t^2\), \(0\le t\le3\).

Solution. \(f'=1-t^2\) and \(g'=2t\), so \(f'^2+g'^2=1-2t^2+t^4+4t^2=1+2t^2+t^4=(1+t^2)^2\). Hence \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2}=1+t^2\) (positive). Then

\[L=\int_0^3(1+t^2)\,dt=\left[t+\frac{t^3}3\right]_0^3=3+9=12.\]

Check. The chord from \((0,0)\) to \((3-9,\,9)=(-6,9)\) has length \(\sqrt{36+81}=\sqrt{117}\approx10.8<12\).

Example 12.1.39: An infinite spiral of finite length

The spiral \(x=e^{-t}\cos t\), \(y=e^{-t}\sin t\), \(t\ge0\), winds around the origin infinitely often. Find its length from \(t=0\) to \(t=T\) and the limit as \(T\to\infty\).

Solution. By the Product Rule \(f'=-e^{-t}\cos t-e^{-t}\sin t=-e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)\) and \(g'=-e^{-t}\sin t+e^{-t}\cos t=e^{-t}(\cos t-\sin t)\). Then

\[f'^2+g'^2=e^{-2t}\bigl[(\cos t+\sin t)^2+(\cos t-\sin t)^2\bigr]=e^{-2t}\bigl[2\cos^2t+2\sin^2t\bigr]=2e^{-2t},\]

so the speed is \(\sqrt2\,e^{-t}\). The length up to \(T\) is \(\int_0^T\sqrt2e^{-t}dt=\sqrt2\left(1-e^{-T}\right)\). As \(T\to\infty\) this tends to \(\sqrt2\) (the improper integral \(\int_0^\infty\sqrt2e^{-t}dt\) converges). The spiral has infinitely many turns but length only \(\sqrt2\approx1.414\), which is plausible because the turns shrink geometrically: each is \(e^{-2\pi}\) times as large as the preceding one, a factor of about \(0.0019\).

items.title: Group 6: Area and surface area
items.text:
Example 12.1.40: An area under a cubic curve

Find the area of the region between the curve \(x=t^2\), \(y=4t-t^3\), \(0\le t\le2\), and the \(x\)-axis.

Solution. \(f'=2t\ge0\), so \(f\) is increasing, and \(g=t(4-t^2)\ge0\) on \([0,2]\). By Theorem 12.1.21,

\[A=\int_0^2(4t-t^3)(2t)\,dt=\int_0^2\left(8t^2-2t^4\right)dt=\left[\frac{8t^3}3-\frac{2t^5}5\right]_0^2=\frac{64}3-\frac{64}5=\frac{128}{15}.\]

Check by Calculus I. Here \(x\) goes from \(0\) to \(4\) and \(t=\sqrt x\), so \(y=4\sqrt x-x^{3/2}\) and \(\int_0^4\left(4x^{1/2}-x^{3/2}\right)dx=\frac83\cdot8-\frac25\cdot32=\frac{64}3-\frac{64}5=\frac{128}{15}\approx8.53\), the same.

Example 12.1.41: A cone, checked by geometry

Revolve the segment \(x=t\), \(y=2t\), \(0\le t\le3\), about the \(x\)-axis and find the surface area by Theorem 12.1.24. Check it with the formula for a cone.

Solution. \(f'=1\), \(g'=2\), speed \(\sqrt5\), and \(g=2t\ge0\). So \(S=\int_0^32\pi(2t)\sqrt5\,dt=4\sqrt5\,\pi\int_0^3t\,dt=4\sqrt5\,\pi\cdot\frac92=18\sqrt5\,\pi\approx126.4\). Check. The cone has base radius \(r=6\) (the value of \(y\) at \(t=3\)) and slant height \(\ell=\sqrt{3^2+6^2}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5\), so its lateral area is \(\pi r\ell=\pi\cdot6\cdot3\sqrt5=18\sqrt5\,\pi\), the same.

Example 12.1.42: The surface of a torus

The circle \(x=5+2\cos t\), \(y=2\sin t\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\), is revolved about the \(y\)-axis. Find the area of the torus.

Solution. The circle has center \((5,0)\) and radius \(2\), so it stays at distance at least \(3\) from the \(y\)-axis and does not cross it, and \(f=5+2\cos t\ge3>0\). The speed is \(\sqrt{(-2\sin t)^2+(2\cos t)^2}=2\). By the \(y\)-axis case of Theorem 12.1.24,

\[S=\int_0^{2\pi}2\pi(5+2\cos t)\cdot2\,dt=4\pi\left[5t+2\sin t\right]_0^{2\pi}=4\pi\cdot10\pi=40\pi^2\approx394.8.\]

In general a torus with tube radius \(r\) and center distance \(R\) has area \(4\pi^2Rr\); here \(R=5\), \(r=2\).

items.title: Group 7: Proofs
items.text:
Example 12.1.43: Two descriptions of the same curve

Prove that the curve \(x=t^2-1\), \(y=t^3-t\), \(-\infty<t<\infty\), is exactly the set of points satisfying \(y^2=x^2(x+1)\).

Plan. Show two inclusions: every point of the parametric curve satisfies the equation, and every solution of the equation comes from some \(t\).

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Let \(x=t^2-1\) and \(y=t^3-t=t(t^2-1)=tx\). Then \(y^2=t^2x^2=(x+1)x^2\), because \(t^2=x+1\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \((x,y)\) satisfy \(y^2=x^2(x+1)\). If \(x\ne0\), put \(t=\frac yx\). Then \(t^2=\frac{y^2}{x^2}=x+1\), so \(x=t^2-1\), and \(y=tx=t(t^2-1)=t^3-t\). If \(x=0\) the equation gives \(y=0\), and \(t=1\) gives \((0,0)\). ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to prove only the first inclusion: that shows the parametric curve is contained in the Cartesian curve, not that it fills it. (Here both are the same, but for \(x=\sin t\), \(y=\sin^2t\) the equation \(y=x^2\) holds on all of the parabola while the curve is only the part with \(\abs x\le1\).)

Example 12.1.44: The tangent line to an ellipse

Let \(a,b>0\) and \(0<t_0<\pi\). Prove that the tangent line to \(x=a\cos t\), \(y=b\sin t\) at \(t=t_0\) is \(\dfrac{x\cos t_0}a+\dfrac{y\sin t_0}b=1\).

Plan. Use Theorem 12.1.12(1) to get the slope, write the point-slope form, and simplify with \(\cos^2+\sin^2=1\).

Proof. \(f'=-a\sin t\), \(g'=b\cos t\), and \(f'(t_0)=-a\sin t_0\ne0\) because \(0<t_0<\pi\). By Theorem 12.1.12(1) the slope is \(-\frac{b\cos t_0}{a\sin t_0}\), and the point is \((a\cos t_0,b\sin t_0)\), so the tangent line is \(y-b\sin t_0=-\frac{b\cos t_0}{a\sin t_0}(x-a\cos t_0)\). Multiply both sides by \(\frac{\sin t_0}b\): \(\frac{y\sin t_0}b-\sin^2t_0=-\frac{x\cos t_0}a+\cos^2t_0\). Move the terms in \(x\) and \(y\) to the left side and the rest to the right: \(\frac{x\cos t_0}a+\frac{y\sin t_0}b=\sin^2t_0+\cos^2t_0=1\). ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to divide by \(f'(t_0)\) when it is zero: at \(t_0=0,\pi\) the tangent is vertical, \(x=\pm a\), which the same formula gives (\(\frac{x\cos t_0}a=1\) means \(x=\pm a\)).

Example 12.1.45: A curve is never shorter than its chord

Prove that the length \(L\) of a curve \(x=f(t)\), \(y=g(t)\), \(a\le t\le b\) (with \(f',g'\) continuous), is at least the distance \(d\) between its endpoints, and that \(L=d\) for a line segment traced from one end to the other at any speed in one direction.

Plan. The partition with only the two points \(t_0=a\) and \(t_1=b\) gives an inscribed polygon that is the chord; apply the last statement of Theorem 12.1.19.

Proof. Take \(\Pi=\{a,b\}\). Its polygon is the single chord from \((f(a),g(a))\) to \((f(b),g(b))\), of length \(d\). By Theorem 12.1.19, \(d=\ell(\Pi)\le L\). For a segment, let \(x=x_0+p\,u(t)\), \(y=y_0+q\,u(t)\) with \(u'\ge0\), \(u(a)=0\) and \(u(b)=1\) (a segment from \(P=(x_0,y_0)\) to \(Q=(x_0+p,y_0+q)\) traced in one direction). Then the speed is \(\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\,u'(t)\) and \(L=\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\int_a^bu'(t)\,dt=\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\bigl(u(b)-u(a)\bigr)=\sqrt{p^2+q^2}=d\). ◻ ∎

A common mistake is to think that the inequality can be an equality for a curved path: it cannot, but proving strictness needs more than we have here. The inequality is the statement that the straight segment is the shortest path between two points.

items.title: Answers and discussion
items.text:
Knowledge Check 12.1.1. From \(y=2t\), \(t=\frac y2\), so \(x=\frac{y^2}4+1\). Since \(-3\le t\le3\), \(-6\le y\le6\). The curve is the part of the parabola \(x=\frac{y^2}4+1\) (vertex \((1,0)\), opening to the right) between \((10,-6)\) and \((10,6)\), traced from bottom to top (\(y=2t\) increases).

Knowledge Check 12.1.2. \(f'=2t\) and \(g'=3t^2\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3t^2}{2t}=\frac{3t}2\) (for \(t\ne0\)). At \(t=2\) the slope is \(3\) (at the point \((4,8)\)).

Knowledge Check 12.1.3. \(f'=3\), \(g'=4\), speed \(\sqrt{9+16}=5\), \(L=\int_0^25\,dt=10\). The endpoints are \((0,0)\) and \((6,8)\), at distance \(\sqrt{36+64}=10\): the same, as it must be for a segment.

items.title: 12.2 Polar Coordinates
items.text:
Download the PDF version

Guiding question

A Cartesian grid is made of two families of straight lines. Many problems are better described by circles and rays: the heat shield of a space vehicle, a radar screen, the orbit of a planet, the sound field around a loudspeaker. For these, the natural address of a point is its distance from a fixed point and the direction in which it lies. That is a polar coordinate system. It has one price: a point no longer has a unique address, and that fact, which looks harmless, decides how we find symmetry, how we find complete curves, and above all how we find where two curves meet. This section builds the system, proves the formulas for converting and for lines and circles, graphs the standard families of polar curves (circles, cardioids and limaçons, roses, lemniscates, spirals), and develops the tests for symmetry, for the complete curve and for intersection points, all proved in full. The calculus of polar curves comes in the next section.

By the end of this section you should be able to:

  • plot a point given in polar coordinates, give all of its polar representations, including those with a negative radial coordinate, and convert between polar and Cartesian coordinates choosing the angle in the correct quadrant;

  • convert equations between polar and Cartesian form, and write polar equations of lines and circles;

  • graph \(r=f(\theta)\) by tables and by the Cartesian-to-polar method, recognize circles, limaçons, roses, lemniscates and spirals, and state the interval of \(\theta\) that traces each curve once;

  • test a polar equation for symmetry, and find the period of a polar curve;

  • find all intersection points of two polar curves, including the points reached at different angles and the origin;

  • prove each of these statements.

items.title: Polar coordinates and their representations
items.text:
Fix a point \(O\), the pole (the origin), and a ray from \(O\), the polar axis, which we draw along the positive \(x\)-axis. Angles are measured counterclockwise from the polar axis, and the ray at angle \( heta\) is the ray from \(O\) through the point \((\cos heta,\sin heta)\).

Definition 12.2.1: Polar coordinates

Let \(r\) and \( heta\) be real numbers. The point \(P(r, heta)\) is defined as follows.

  • If \(r>0\): the point on the ray at angle \( heta\) whose distance from \(O\) is \(r\).

  • If \(r<0\): the point on the ray at angle \( heta+\pi\) (the ray opposite to the ray at angle \( heta\)) whose distance from \(O\) is \(\abs r\).

  • If \(r=0\): the point \(O\).

We call \((r, heta)\) a polar representation (or a pair of polar coordinates) of \(P(r, heta)\). The number \(r\) is the radial coordinate, a signed distance, and \( heta\) is the angular coordinate.

The picture is drawn for \(r=2.4\) and \( heta= rac\pi6\): \(P^*(-r, heta)\) is the reflection of \(P(r, heta)\) through the origin. Polar coordinates agree with Cartesian coordinates in the following precise sense.

Theorem 12.2.2: Conversion between polar and Cartesian coordinates

The point \(P(r, heta)\), for every real \(r\) (positive, negative or zero), has Cartesian coordinates

\[x=r\cos heta,\qquad y=r\sin heta.\]

Consequently \(x^2+y^2=r^2\), and \( an heta= rac yx\) if \(x e0\).

Proof. Case \(r>0\). The ray at angle \( heta\) passes through the point \((\cos heta,\sin heta)\), which is at distance \(\sqrt{\cos^2 heta+\sin^2 heta}=1\) from \(O\). The point on this ray at distance \(r\) is \(r\) times this point: \((r\cos heta,r\sin heta)\). Case \(r<0\). By definition the point is on the ray at angle \( heta+\pi\), at distance \(\abs r=-r\). By the case just proved it is \( igl(\abs r\cos( heta+\pi),\abs r\sin( heta+\pi) igr)\). Since \(\cos( heta+\pi)=-\cos heta\) and \(\sin( heta+\pi)=-\sin heta\), and \(\abs r=-r\), this is \((-r\cdot(-\cos heta),\,-r\cdot(-\sin heta))=(r\cos heta,r\sin heta)\). Case \(r=0\). Both sides are \((0,0)\). The consequences. \(x^2+y^2=r^2\cos^2 heta+r^2\sin^2 heta=r^2(\cos^2 heta+\sin^2 heta)=r^2\). If \(x e0\) then \(r e0\) and \(\cos heta e0\), and \( rac yx= rac{r\sin heta}{r\cos heta}= an heta\). ◻ ∎

A single point has many representations: we can add a full turn to \( heta\), and we can replace \((r, heta)\) by \((-r, heta+\pi)\). The next theorem says that these are the only changes.

Theorem 12.2.3: All the representations of a point

  1. The origin \(O\) has the representations \((0, heta)\), for every real \( heta\), and no others.

  2. Let \(P e O\) have Cartesian coordinates \((x,y)\) and put \( ho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0\). Then there is an angle \( heta_0\) with \(\cos heta_0= rac x ho\) and \(\sin heta_0= rac y ho\), and the representations of \(P\) are exactly

    \[( ho,\ heta_0+2\pi k)\quad ext{and}\quad(- ho,\ heta_0+\pi+2\pi k),\qquad k=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots\]

Proof. By Theorem 12.2.2, \((r, heta)\) represents the point \((x,y)\) exactly when \(r\cos heta=x\) and \(r\sin heta=y\). (1) For \((x,y)=(0,0)\) these equations say \(r\cos heta=0=r\sin heta\). Since \(\cos heta\) and \(\sin heta\) are never both \(0\) (because \(\cos^2 heta+\sin^2 heta=1\)), this forces \(r=0\), and then any \( heta\) works. (2) Existence of \( heta_0\). Put \(u= rac x ho\) and \(v= rac y ho\), so \(u^2+v^2=1\) and \(\abs u\le1\). Let \( heta_0=\arccos u\) if \(v\ge0\) and \( heta_0=-\arccos u\) if \(v<0\). Then \(\cos heta_0=u\) in both cases (cosine is even). Also \(\sin(\arccos u)=\sqrt{1-u^2}=\abs v\). If \(v\ge0\), \(\sin heta_0=\abs v=v\); if \(v<0\), \(\sin heta_0=-\abs v=v\). All the representations. Let \((r, heta)\) represent \(P\). Squaring the two equations and adding, \(r^2=x^2+y^2= ho^2\), so \(r= ho\) or \(r=- ho\). If \(r= ho\), then \(\cos heta= rac x ho=\cos heta_0\) and \(\sin heta=\sin heta_0\). By the subtraction formula,

\[\cos( heta- heta_0)=\cos heta\cos heta_0+\sin heta\sin heta_0=\cos^2 heta_0+\sin^2 heta_0=1,\]

and the cosine equals \(1\) only at the multiples of \(2\pi\), so \( heta= heta_0+2\pi k\). If \(r=- ho\), then \(\cos heta=- rac x ho=\cos( heta_0+\pi)\) and \(\sin heta=- rac y ho=\sin( heta_0+\pi)\), and the same argument with \( heta_0+\pi\) in place of \( heta_0\) gives \( heta= heta_0+\pi+2\pi k\). Conversely, each pair in the list satisfies \(r\cos heta=x\) and \(r\sin heta=y\), because sine and cosine have period \(2\pi\) and \(\cos( heta_0+\pi)=-\cos heta_0\), \(\sin( heta_0+\pi)=-\sin heta_0\). ◻ ∎

Procedure 12.2.4: From Cartesian to polar coordinates

Given \((x,y) e(0,0)\):

  1. Compute \( ho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).

  2. Find an angle \( heta_0\) with \(\cos heta_0= rac x ho\) and \(\sin heta_0= rac y ho\). Decide the quadrant from the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) first; use a reference angle (\(\arctan rac{\abs y}{\abs x}\)) and place it in that quadrant.

  3. The representations are \(( ho, heta_0+2\pi k)\) and \((- ho, heta_0+\pi+2\pi k)\).

  4. Check by converting back: \( ho\cos heta_0=x\) and \( ho\sin heta_0=y\).

The origin is \((0, heta)\) for any \( heta\).

The tangent relation alone is not enough

\( an heta= rac yx\) has solutions in two opposite quadrants, and a calculator’s \(\arctan rac yx\) always returns an angle between \(- rac\pi2\) and \( rac\pi2\), which is correct only when \(x>0\). For \((-1,1)\) the value \(\arctan(-1)=- rac\pi4\) points into the fourth quadrant, but the point is in the second: \( heta_0= rac{3\pi}4\). Always look at the signs of \(x\) and \(y\).

Example 12.2.5: Points in polar coordinates

Plot the points \(A\left(2, rac{7\pi}6 ight)\), \(B\left(-3, rac\pi4 ight)\) and \(C\left(-2,- rac{2\pi}3 ight)\). For each, give its Cartesian coordinates and two other polar representations.

Solution. Locating the points. \(A\): \(r=2>0\), so \(A\) is on the ray at angle \( rac{7\pi}6=210^\circ\) (in the third quadrant, \(30^\circ\) past the negative \(x\)-axis) at distance \(2\). \(B\): \(r=-3<0\), so first find the ray at angle \( rac\pi4\), then go to the opposite ray (angle \( rac\pi4+\pi= rac{5\pi}4\)), at distance \(3\); \(B\) is in the third quadrant. \(C\): \(r=-2<0\) and \( heta=- rac{2\pi}3\) is \(120^\circ\) clockwise; the opposite ray has angle \(- rac{2\pi}3+\pi= rac\pi3\), so \(C\) is on the ray at \(60^\circ\), at distance \(2\), in the first quadrant (Figure below).

Cartesian coordinates (Theorem 12.2.2). For \(A\): \(\cos rac{7\pi}6=- rac{\sqrt3}2\) and \(\sin rac{7\pi}6=- rac12\), so \(A=\left(2\cdot\left(- rac{\sqrt3}2 ight),\,2\cdot\left(- rac12 ight) ight)=(-\sqrt3,-1)\). For \(B\): \(\cos rac\pi4=\sin rac\pi4= rac{\sqrt2}2\), so \(B=\left(-3\cdot rac{\sqrt2}2,\,-3\cdot rac{\sqrt2}2 ight)=\left(- rac{3\sqrt2}2,- rac{3\sqrt2}2 ight)\approx(-2.12,-2.12)\). For \(C\): \(\cos\left(- rac{2\pi}3 ight)=- rac12\) and \(\sin\left(- rac{2\pi}3 ight)=- rac{\sqrt3}2\), so \(C=\left(-2\cdot\left(- rac12 ight),\,-2\cdot\left(- rac{\sqrt3}2 ight) ight)=(1,\sqrt3)\).

Other representations (Theorem 12.2.3: subtract \(2\pi\), or change the sign of \(r\) and add or subtract \(\pi\)). \(A\): \(\left(2, rac{7\pi}6-2\pi ight)=\left(2,- rac{5\pi}6 ight)\) and \(\left(-2, rac{7\pi}6-\pi ight)=\left(-2, rac\pi6 ight)\). \(B\): \(\left(3, rac\pi4+\pi ight)=\left(3, rac{5\pi}4 ight)\) and \(\left(-3, rac\pi4-2\pi ight)=\left(-3,- rac{7\pi}4 ight)\). \(C\): \(\left(2,- rac{2\pi}3+\pi ight)=\left(2, rac\pi3 ight)\) and \(\left(-2,- rac{2\pi}3+2\pi ight)=\left(-2, rac{4\pi}3 ight)\). Check. Convert \(\left(-2, rac\pi6 ight)\): \(\left(-2\cdot rac{\sqrt3}2,-2\cdot rac12 ight)=(-\sqrt3,-1)=A\); and \(\left(2, rac\pi3 ight)\): \(\left(2\cdot rac12,2\cdot rac{\sqrt3}2 ight)=(1,\sqrt3)=C\).

The dashed rays show the angle that was given for \(B\) and for \(C\); because \(r<0\), the point is on the opposite ray.

Example 12.2.6: Converting coordinates

(a) Convert the polar points \(P\left(-4, rac{2\pi}3 ight)\) and \(Q\left(6,- rac{5\pi}4 ight)\) to Cartesian coordinates. (b) Convert the Cartesian points \((-3,-3\sqrt3)\), \((-2,1)\) and \((0,-5)\) to polar coordinates, giving one representation with \(r>0\) and one with \(r<0\).

Solution. (a) \(P\). \(\cos rac{2\pi}3=- rac12\) and \(\sin rac{2\pi}3= rac{\sqrt3}2\), so \(x=-4\cdot\left(- rac12 ight)=2\) and \(y=-4\cdot rac{\sqrt3}2=-2\sqrt3\): \(P=(2,-2\sqrt3)\approx(2,-3.46)\). \(Q\). \(\cos\left(- rac{5\pi}4 ight)=\cos rac{5\pi}4=- rac{\sqrt2}2\) and \(\sin\left(- rac{5\pi}4 ight)=-\sin rac{5\pi}4= rac{\sqrt2}2\), so \(Q=\left(6\cdot\left(- rac{\sqrt2}2 ight),\,6\cdot rac{\sqrt2}2 ight)=\left(-3\sqrt2,3\sqrt2 ight)\). (b) \((-3,-3\sqrt3)\). \( ho=\sqrt{9+27}=\sqrt{36}=6\). Both coordinates are negative, so the point is in the third quadrant. \(\cos heta_0= rac{-3}6=- rac12\) and \(\sin heta_0= rac{-3\sqrt3}6=- rac{\sqrt3}2\): the reference angle is \( rac\pi3\), so \( heta_0=\pi+ rac\pi3= rac{4\pi}3\). Representations: \(\left(6, rac{4\pi}3 ight)\) and \(\left(-6, rac{4\pi}3-\pi ight)=\left(-6, rac\pi3 ight)\). Check: \(6\cos rac{4\pi}3=-3\), \(6\sin rac{4\pi}3=-3\sqrt3\). \((-2,1)\). \( ho=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5\). The point is in the second quadrant (\(x<0\), \(y>0\)), with \( an heta=- rac12\). The calculator value \(\arctan\left(- rac12 ight)\approx-0.4636\) is in the fourth quadrant, so we must add \(\pi\): \( heta_0=\pi-\arctan rac12\approx3.1416-0.4636=2.6779\). Representations: \(\left(\sqrt5,\,\pi-\arctan frac12 ight)\) and \(\left(-\sqrt5,\,-\arctan frac12 ight)\) (subtract \(\pi\) from \( heta_0\)). Check: \(\sqrt5\cos(2.6779)\approx-2.000\) and \(\sqrt5\sin(2.6779)\approx1.000\). \((0,-5)\). \( ho=5\), and \( rac y ho=-1\), \( rac x ho=0\), so \( heta_0=- rac\pi2\) (\( an heta\) is undefined here; the signs and the unit vector \((0,-1)\) decide). Representations: \(\left(5,- rac\pi2 ight)\) and \(\left(-5, rac\pi2 ight)\).

Knowledge Check 12.2.1: Same point or not

Which of the pairs \(\left(2, rac\pi3 ight)\), \(\left(-2, rac{4\pi}3 ight)\), \(\left(2, rac{7\pi}3 ight)\), \(\left(-2,- rac\pi3 ight)\) represent the same point as \(\left(2, rac\pi3 ight)\)?

items.title: Distance, equations, lines and circles
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.7: The distance formula in polar coordinates

For any real \(r_1,r_2, heta_1, heta_2\), the distance \(d\) between \(P_1(r_1, heta_1)\) and \(P_2(r_2, heta_2)\) satisfies

\[d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2-2r_1r_2\cos( heta_1- heta_2).\]

Proof. By Theorem 12.2.2, \(P_1=(r_1\cos heta_1,r_1\sin heta_1)\) and \(P_2=(r_2\cos heta_2,r_2\sin heta_2)\). The distance formula gives

\[ egin{aligned} d^2&=(r_1\cos heta_1-r_2\cos heta_2)^2+(r_1\sin heta_1-r_2\sin heta_2)^2\ &=r_1^2\cos^2 heta_1-2r_1r_2\cos heta_1\cos heta_2+r_2^2\cos^2 heta_2+r_1^2\sin^2 heta_1-2r_1r_2\sin heta_1\sin heta_2+r_2^2\sin^2 heta_2\ &=r_1^2\left(\cos^2 heta_1+\sin^2 heta_1 ight)+r_2^2\left(\cos^2 heta_2+\sin^2 heta_2 ight)-2r_1r_2\left(\cos heta_1\cos heta_2+\sin heta_1\sin heta_2 ight)\ &=r_1^2+r_2^2-2r_1r_2\cos( heta_1- heta_2), \end{aligned}\]

where the last step uses \(\cos^2+\sin^2=1\) and the subtraction formula for the cosine. (This is the law of cosines.) ◻ ∎

Definition 12.2.8: The graph of a polar equation

The graph of a polar equation \(E(r, heta)=0\) (for example \(r=f( heta)\)) is the set of all points \(P\) for which at least one polar representation \((r, heta)\) of \(P\) satisfies the equation.

Because a point has infinitely many representations, a point can be on the graph even though the representation you happened to write down does not satisfy the equation. For instance \(\left(-1, rac{3\pi}2 ight)\) does not satisfy \(r=1+\cos heta\) (the right side is \(1+0=1\)), yet it represents the same point as \(\left(1, rac\pi2 ight)\), which does: the point \((0,-1)\) is on the graph of \(r=1+\cos heta\). The next theorem tells when an equation can be converted without such surprises.

Theorem 12.2.9: Converting equations

  1. Let \(F(x,y)=0\) be a Cartesian equation and \(E(r, heta)=F(r\cos heta,r\sin heta)\). A point is on the graph of \(E(r, heta)=0\) exactly when it satisfies \(F(x,y)=0\), and then every representation of the point satisfies \(E=0\).

  2. The graph of \(r\,E(r, heta)=0\) is the graph of \(E(r, heta)=0\) together with the origin.

Proof. (1) Let \((r, heta)\) be any representation of the point \(P=(x,y)\). By Theorem 12.2.2, \(E(r, heta)=F(r\cos heta,r\sin heta)=F(x,y)\), which does not depend on which representation we chose. So \(E=0\) holds for one representation if and only if \(F(x,y)=0\), if and only if it holds for all. (2) A pair \((r, heta)\) satisfies \(rE(r, heta)=0\) exactly when \(r=0\) or \(E(r, heta)=0\). The pairs with \(r=0\) represent the origin, so the origin is on the graph of \(rE=0\). A point \(P e O\) has only representations with \(r e0\) (Theorem 12.2.3), so it is on the graph of \(rE=0\) exactly when some representation satisfies \(E=0\), that is, when it is on the graph of \(E=0\). ◻ ∎

So multiplying by \(r\) can add only the origin, and it adds nothing when the origin is already on the graph. Dividing by \(r\) can lose only the origin, and it loses nothing when the origin is on the graph of the new equation.

Theorem 12.2.10: Lines in polar coordinates

  1. The graph of \( heta=\alpha\) is the line through \(O\) that contains the ray at angle \(\alpha\) (slope \( an\alpha\), or the \(y\)-axis if \(\cos\alpha=0\)).

  2. The vertical line \(x=h\) has the polar equation \(r\cos heta=h\) and the horizontal line \(y=k\) has \(r\sin heta=k\).

  3. Normal form. Let \(p>0\). The line whose point nearest to \(O\) is \(P(p,\alpha)\) is the graph of \(r\cos( heta-\alpha)=p\).

  4. If \(b e0\), the line \(y=mx+b\) is the graph of \(r=\dfrac{b}{\sin heta-m\cos heta}\).

Proof. (1) The graph is the set of points \(P(r,\alpha)\), \(r\) real. By Theorem 12.2.2 this is \(\{r(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\}\), the line through \(O\) with direction vector \((\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\). (2) Apply Theorem 12.2.9(1) to \(x-h=0\) and \(y-k=0\). (3) Let \(\mathbf n=(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\), a unit vector. The foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) is \(p\,\mathbf n=(p\cos\alpha,p\sin\alpha)=P(p,\alpha)\), and the line through it perpendicular to \(\mathbf n\) is \(\{X:\ \mathbf n\cdot(X-p\mathbf n)=0\}=\{X:\ \mathbf n\cdot X=p\}\), because \(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n=1\). In coordinates this is \(x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=p\). Now put \(x=r\cos heta\), \(y=r\sin heta\):

\[x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=r\cos heta\cos\alpha+r\sin heta\sin\alpha=r\cos( heta-\alpha).\]

By Theorem 12.2.9(1) the line is the graph of \(r\cos( heta-\alpha)=p\). (4) By Theorem 12.2.9(1), \(y=mx+b\) becomes \(r\sin heta=mr\cos heta+b\), that is \(r(\sin heta-m\cos heta)=b\). If \(\sin heta=m\cos heta\) this reads \(0=b\), which is false, so no point has such an angle; for every other \( heta\) the equation is \(r= rac b{\sin heta-m\cos heta}\). ◻ ∎

Theorem 12.2.11: Circles in polar coordinates

  1. For \(a e0\), the graph of \(r=a\) is the circle of radius \(\abs a\) centered at \(O\).

  2. The circle of radius \(R\) whose center is \(C( ho_0, heta_0)\) is the graph of

    \[r^2-2 ho_0\,r\cos( heta- heta_0)=R^2- ho_0^2 .\]

    If the center is the Cartesian point \((a,b)\), this reads \(r^2-2r(a\cos heta+b\sin heta)=R^2-a^2-b^2\).

  3. If \((a,b) e(0,0)\), the graph of \(r=2a\cos heta+2b\sin heta\) is the whole circle of radius \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) centered at \((a,b)\), which passes through the origin. In particular \(r=2a\cos heta\) is the circle with center \((a,0)\) and radius \(\abs a\), and \(r=2b\sin heta\) is the circle with center \((0,b)\) and radius \(\abs b\).

Proof. (1) A point is on the graph if some representation has \(r=a\); its distance from \(O\) is then \(\abs a\). Conversely, a point at distance \(\abs a\) from \(O\) has the representations \((\abs a, heta_0)\) and \((-\abs a, heta_0+\pi)\) (Theorem 12.2.3), and one of them has radial coordinate \(a\). (2) The point \(P(r, heta)\) is on the circle exactly when \(\abs{PC}^2=R^2\). By Theorem 12.2.7, \(\abs{PC}^2=r^2+ ho_0^2-2r ho_0\cos( heta- heta_0)\), so the condition is \(r^2-2 ho_0r\cos( heta- heta_0)=R^2- ho_0^2\). The distance does not depend on the representation chosen, so the equation holds for one representation of \(P\) exactly when it holds for all. If \(C=(a,b)\) then \(a= ho_0\cos heta_0\) and \(b= ho_0\sin heta_0\), and \( ho_0\cos( heta- heta_0)= ho_0\cos heta\cos heta_0+ ho_0\sin heta\sin heta_0=a\cos heta+b\sin heta\). (3) Here \(R^2=a^2+b^2\), so the right side of the equation in (2) is \(0\) and the equation is \(r igl(r-2a\cos heta-2b\sin heta igr)=0\). By Theorem 12.2.9(2), the graph of \(r=2a\cos heta+2b\sin heta\) is the circle, provided the origin is on the graph of \(r=2a\cos heta+2b\sin heta\). It is: \(2a\cos heta+2b\sin heta=0\) when \((\cos heta,\sin heta)= rac1{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}(-b,a)\), an angle that exists because this is a unit vector, and then \(r=0\). (Equivalently, the circle passes through \(O\) because \(\abs{OC}=R\).) ◻ ∎

Example 12.2.12: Converting equations

Convert to the other coordinate system and identify the graph: (a) \(r=6\cos heta-8\sin heta\); (b) \(r^2\cos2 heta=8\); (c) \(y=2x^2\); (d) \(3x-4y=12\).

Solution. (a) Multiply by \(r\) (see Theorem 12.2.9(2)): \(r^2=6r\cos heta-8r\sin heta\). Substitute \(r^2=x^2+y^2\), \(r\cos heta=x\), \(r\sin heta=y\): \(x^2+y^2=6x-8y\). Collect and complete the squares:

\[x^2-6x+9+y^2+8y+16=9+16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-3)^2+(y+4)^2=25.\]

This is the circle with center \((3,-4)\) and radius \(5\), which agrees with Theorem 12.2.11(3) for \(2a=6\), \(2b=-8\). Multiplying by \(r\) could have added the origin, but the origin is already on the graph of the original equation, since \(6\cos heta-8\sin heta=0\) at \( heta=\arctan rac34\). So the equation \(r=6\cos heta-8\sin heta\) describes the whole circle. Check. \( heta=0\): \(r=6\), the point \((6,0)\), and \((6-3)^2+(0+4)^2=9+16=25\). \( heta= rac\pi2\): \(r=-8\), the point \(P\left(-8, rac\pi2 ight)=(0,-8)\), and \((0-3)^2+(-8+4)^2=9+16=25\). (b) Use \(\cos2 heta=\cos^2 heta-\sin^2 heta\): \(r^2\cos^2 heta-r^2\sin^2 heta=8\), that is \(x^2-y^2=8\), a hyperbola with vertices \((\pm2\sqrt2,0)\) and asymptotes \(y=\pm x\). No multiplication was needed, so Theorem 12.2.9(1) shows that the graphs agree. (c) \(y=2x^2\) becomes \(r\sin heta=2r^2\cos^2 heta\), that is \(r\left(\sin heta-2r\cos^2 heta ight)=0\). So \(r=0\) or \(r=\dfrac{\sin heta}{2\cos^2 heta}=\dfrac12 an heta\sec heta\). The origin is on the graph of the second equation (\( heta=0\) gives \(r=0\)), so the single equation \(r= rac12 an heta\sec heta\) describes the whole parabola. Check. \( heta= rac\pi4\): \(r= rac{\sqrt2/2}{2\cdot rac12}= rac{\sqrt2}2\), the point \(\left( rac{\sqrt2}2\cos rac\pi4, rac{\sqrt2}2\sin rac\pi4 ight)=\left( rac12, rac12 ight)\), and \(2\left( rac12 ight)^2= rac12\). (d) Substitute \(x=r\cos heta\), \(y=r\sin heta\): \(r(3\cos heta-4\sin heta)=12\). Divide by \(\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\): \(r\left( rac35\cos heta- rac45\sin heta ight)= rac{12}5\). The numbers \( rac35,- rac45\) satisfy \( rac9{25}+ rac{16}{25}=1\), so \(\cos\alpha= rac35\), \(\sin\alpha=- rac45\) for an angle \(\alpha=-\arctan rac43\approx-0.9273\), and the left side is \(r\cos( heta-\alpha)\). By Theorem 12.2.10(3):

\[r\cos( heta-\alpha)= rac{12}5,\]

the line whose nearest point to \(O\) is \(P\left( rac{12}5,\alpha ight)=\left( rac{36}{25},- rac{48}{25} ight)\). Check. \(3\cdot rac{36}{25}-4\cdot\left(- rac{48}{25} ight)= rac{108+192}{25}=12\), and the distance from \(O\) to \(3x-4y=12\) is \( rac{12}{\sqrt{9+16}}= rac{12}5\).

Knowledge Check 12.2.2: A circle from its equation

Describe the graph of \(r=-3\sin heta\): give its center and radius.

Pause and think 12.2.1: Multiplying by \(r\)

In Example 12.2.12(a) we multiplied the equation by \(r\), and Theorem 12.2.9(2) says that this may add the origin. No point was added there. Give an equation whose graph does not contain the origin, and show that multiplying it by \(r\) does add the origin.

Answer and discussion

Take \(r=1\), the unit circle, which does not contain the origin. Multiplying by \(r\) gives \(r^2=r\), that is \(r(r-1)=0\), whose graph contains all the points with \(r=0\): the origin is added. This is Theorem 12.2.9(2) with \(E=r-1\): \(rE=r(r-1)\).

items.title: A polar curve is a parametric curve
items.text:
A polar equation \(r=f( heta)\) describes a curve in the plane, and Section 12.1 gave us the language for curves: parameter, orientation, tangent line. The two descriptions are connected by one theorem.

Theorem 12.2.13: A polar curve is a parametric curve

Let \(f\) be defined on an interval \(I\) (possibly all of \(\R\)). The points \(P(f( heta), heta)\), \( heta\) in \(I\), form the parametric curve (Definition 12.1.1)

\[x=f( heta)\cos heta,\qquad y=f( heta)\sin heta,\qquad heta\in I,\]

with \( heta\) as the parameter; its positive orientation is the direction of increasing \( heta\). If \(f\) is differentiable, then

\[x'( heta)=f'( heta)\cos heta-f( heta)\sin heta,\qquad y'( heta)=f'( heta)\sin heta+f( heta)\cos heta,\]

and \(x'( heta)^2+y'( heta)^2=f( heta)^2+f'( heta)^2\). If \(f( heta_0)=0\) and \(f'( heta_0) e0\), the curve passes through the origin at \( heta= heta_0\) and its tangent line there is the line \( heta= heta_0\).

Proof. The coordinates are those of Theorem 12.2.2 with \(r=f( heta)\). By the Product Rule, \(x'=f'\cos heta-f\sin heta\) and \(y'=f'\sin heta+f\cos heta\). Squaring and adding,

\[ egin{aligned} x'^2+y'^2&=f'^2\cos^2 heta-2ff'\sin heta\cos heta+f^2\sin^2 heta+f'^2\sin^2 heta+2ff'\sin heta\cos heta+f^2\cos^2 heta\ &=f'^2\left(\cos^2 heta+\sin^2 heta ight)+f^2\left(\sin^2 heta+\cos^2 heta ight)=f'^2+f^2, \end{aligned}\]

since the two cross terms cancel. Now let \(f( heta_0)=0\) and \(f'( heta_0) e0\). Then \(x( heta_0)=y( heta_0)=0\), so the curve is at \(O\), and the velocity is \( igl(x'( heta_0),y'( heta_0) igr)=f'( heta_0)\,(\cos heta_0,\sin heta_0) e(0,0)\). By Theorem 12.1.12, if \(x'( heta_0) e0\) (that is, \(\cos heta_0 e0\)) the tangent line has slope \( rac{y'}{x'}= rac{\sin heta_0}{\cos heta_0}= an heta_0\) and passes through \(O\); if \(x'( heta_0)=0\) the tangent line is vertical through \(O\). In both cases it is the line through \(O\) at angle \( heta_0\), the graph of \( heta= heta_0\) (Theorem 12.2.10(1)). ◻ ∎

When \(f( heta_0)=0=f'( heta_0)\) the velocity vanishes and the theorem says nothing; the cardioid of the next pages has such a point. The identity \(x'^2+y'^2=f^2+f'^2\) will matter when we measure lengths of polar curves; for now we use only the last statement, which tells us in which direction a curve leaves the origin.

Procedure 12.2.14: The Cartesian-to-polar method for graphing \(r=f( heta)\)

  1. Graph \(r=f( heta)\) in an ordinary \( heta r\)-plane over an interval of \( heta\) that traces the whole curve (see Theorem 12.2.23 for how long such an interval must be).

  2. Mark the zeros of \(f\) (the curve passes through the origin; by Theorem 12.2.13 it is tangent to the line \( heta= heta_0\) if \(f'( heta_0) e0\)) and the extreme values of \(\abs f\) (the farthest points).

  3. Where \(r>0\) the point is on the ray at angle \( heta\). Where \(r<0\) it is on the opposite ray, at distance \(\abs r\).

  4. Where \(\abs r\) increases the curve moves away from the origin; where it decreases, towards it. Follow the curve in the order of increasing \( heta\), and draw the arrows.

Example 12.2.15: A limaçon with an inner loop

Graph \(r=1+2\cos heta\) for \(0\le heta\le2\pi\) with the Cartesian-to-polar method. Find where it meets the origin, the tangent lines there, and any symmetry.

Solution. The \( heta r\)-graph. \(f( heta)=1+2\cos heta\) is a cosine curve with amplitude \(2\), shifted up \(1\): \(f(0)=3\) is the maximum and \(f(\pi)=-1\) the minimum. Zeros. \(1+2\cos heta=0\) gives \(\cos heta=- rac12\), so \( heta= rac{2\pi}3\) and \( heta= rac{4\pi}3\) in \([0,2\pi]\). Sign. \(f>0\) for \(0\le heta< rac{2\pi}3\) and for \( rac{4\pi}3< heta\le2\pi\), and \(f<0\) for \( rac{2\pi}3< heta< rac{4\pi}3\). Table.

\[ egin{array}{c|ccccccccc} heta&0& rac\pi3& rac\pi2& rac{2\pi}3&\pi& rac{4\pi}3& rac{3\pi}2& rac{5\pi}3&2\pi\\hline r&3&2&1&0&-1&0&1&2&3\ ext{point}&A&B&C&D&E&F&G&H&A \end{array}\]

Transfer to the polar plane. For \(0\le heta< rac{2\pi}3\), \(r>0\) decreases from \(3\) to \(0\): the curve starts at \(A=(3,0)\), passes \(B=2\left(\cos rac\pi3,\sin rac\pi3 ight)=(1,\sqrt3)\) and \(C=(0,1)\), and reaches the origin at \(D\) along the ray \( heta= rac{2\pi}3\). For \( rac{2\pi}3< heta< rac{4\pi}3\) we have \(r<0\), so the points are on the opposite rays, with angles between \( rac{2\pi}3+\pi= rac{5\pi}3\) and \( rac{4\pi}3+\pi= rac{7\pi}3\equiv rac\pi3\), which is to the right of the origin. The distance \(\abs r\) grows from \(0\) to \(1\) at \( heta=\pi\) and shrinks back to \(0\): the farthest point of this inner loop is \(E=P(-1,\pi)=(-1\cdot\cos\pi,-1\cdot\sin\pi)=(1,0)\). At \(F\) the curve is again at the origin. For \( rac{4\pi}3< heta\le2\pi\) we have \(r>0\), increasing from \(0\) to \(3\): through \(G=(0,-1)\) and \(H=2\left(\cos rac{5\pi}3,\sin rac{5\pi}3 ight)=(1,-\sqrt3)\) back to \(A\). Tangents at the origin. \(f'( heta)=-2\sin heta\), and \(f'\left( rac{2\pi}3 ight)=-\sqrt3 e0\), \(f'\left( rac{4\pi}3 ight)=\sqrt3 e0\). By Theorem 12.2.13 the tangent lines at \(O\) are \( heta= rac{2\pi}3\) (slope \( an rac{2\pi}3=-\sqrt3\)) and \( heta= rac{4\pi}3\) (slope \( an rac{4\pi}3=\sqrt3\)). Symmetry. \(f(- heta)=f( heta)\), so the curve is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis (Theorem 12.2.21 below), which agrees with the picture.

Answer. A limaçon with an inner loop: an outer loop through \((3,0)\), \((0,\pm1)\) and the origin, and an inner loop from the origin to \((1,0)\) and back, traced for \( rac{2\pi}3\le heta\le rac{4\pi}3\) (Figure below).

The tangent lines at the origin, \( heta= rac{2\pi}3\) and \( heta= rac{4\pi}3\), are the dashed lines. The left graph and the right curve are the same information: the red part of the \( heta r\)-graph, where \(r<0\), becomes the inner loop.

Pause and think 12.2.2: An inner loop on the right

The inner loop of \(r=1+2\cos heta\) is traced for \( rac{2\pi}3\le heta\le rac{4\pi}3\), angles that point into the left half-plane. Why does the loop lie in the right half-plane?

Answer and discussion

For \( rac{2\pi}3< heta< rac{4\pi}3\) the radial coordinate is negative, so each point is on the ray opposite to the direction \( heta\), that is at the angle \( heta+\pi\). As \( heta\) runs from \( rac{2\pi}3\) to \( rac{4\pi}3\), \( heta+\pi\) runs from \( rac{5\pi}3\) to \( rac{7\pi}3\), angles that point into the right half-plane (they are within \( rac\pi3\) of the positive \(x\)-axis). At the middle, \( heta=\pi\), the point is \(P(-1,\pi)=(1,0)\).

items.title: The limaçon family
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.16: Limaçons

Let \(a>0\), \(b>0\) and consider the curve \(r=a+b\cos\theta\) (the curve \(r=a+b\sin\theta\) is this one rotated through \(\frac\pi2\)). It is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis, and its shape depends on \(\frac ab\):

  1. \(a<b\): inner loop. \(r\) changes sign, so the curve passes through \(O\) at \(\cos\theta=-\frac ab\) and has an inner loop traced where \(r<0\).

  2. \(a=b\): cardioid. \(r\ge0\) and \(r=0\) only at \(\theta=\pi\), where the velocity is zero: a cusp at \(O\).

  3. \(b<a<2b\): dimple. \(r>0\), and along the upper half \(0\le\theta\le\pi\) the coordinate \(x\) first decreases, then increases.

  4. \(a\ge2b\): oval. \(r>0\) and \(x\) decreases steadily along the upper half.

Proof. \(f(\theta)=a+b\cos\theta\) is even, so the curve is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis (Theorem 12.2.21 below). The zeros of \(f\) are the solutions of \(\cos\theta=-\frac ab\), which exist exactly when \(a\le b\). (1) If \(a<b\), then \(f\) is positive near \(\theta=0\) and negative at \(\theta=\pi\) (\(f(\pi)=a-b<0\)), so it changes sign at the zeros \(\theta=\pm\theta_0\), \(\theta_0=\arccos\left(-\frac ab\right)\), where \(f'(\theta)=-b\sin\theta\ne0\); for \(\theta_0<\theta<2\pi-\theta_0\) we have \(r<0\), and these points form the inner loop (Procedure 12.2.14). (2) If \(a=b\), then \(f(\theta)=b(1+\cos\theta)=2b\cos^2\frac\theta2\ge0\), which is \(0\) only when \(\cos\frac\theta2=0\), that is at \(\theta=\pi\) (mod \(2\pi\)). There \(f(\pi)=0\) and \(f'(\pi)=-b\sin\pi=0\), so the velocity \((x',y')=(0,0)\) by Theorem 12.2.13. (3), (4) If \(a>b\) then \(f(\theta)\ge a-b>0\). On the curve \(x=r\cos\theta=a\cos\theta+b\cos^2\theta\), hence

\[\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta-2b\sin\theta\cos\theta=-\sin\theta\,(a+2b\cos\theta).\]

On \(0<\theta<\pi\), \(\sin\theta>0\), so the sign of \(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\) is the sign of \(-(a+2b\cos\theta)\). If \(a\ge2b\) then \(a+2b\cos\theta>a-2b\ge0\) for \(\cos\theta>-1\), so \(x\) decreases on \([0,\pi]\): (4). If \(a<2b\), then \(a+2b\cos\theta=0\) at \(\cos\theta=-\frac a{2b}\in(-1,0)\), an angle \(\theta_1\) in \(\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right)\), positive before \(\theta_1\) and negative after: so \(\frac{dx}{d\theta}<0\) on \((0,\theta_1)\) and \(>0\) on \((\theta_1,\pi)\), and \(x\) decreases and then increases: (3). ◻ ∎

The four curves are \(r=a+2\cos\theta\) with \(a=1,2,3,4\). The red point is the one at \(\theta=\pi\), where \(r=a-2\): \((1,0)\) (tip of the inner loop), the cusp \(O\), the dimple \((-1,0)\) and the point \((-2,0)\).

items.title: Roses
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.17: Roses

Let \(m\) be a positive integer and \(a\ne0\). The graph of \(r=a\cos m\theta\) is a rose made of congruent petals, each a closed loop through the origin whose tip is at distance \(\abs a\) from \(O\); adjacent petals meet only at \(O\). There are \(m\) petals if \(m\) is odd (traced once for \(0\le\theta\le\pi\)) and \(2m\) petals if \(m\) is even (traced once for \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\)).

The tips are at the angles \(\frac{n\pi}m\) with \(n\) even if \(m\) is odd (and \(a>0\)), and with \(n\) any integer if \(m\) is even. The graph of \(r=a\sin m\theta\) is the same rose rotated through the angle \(\frac\pi{2m}\).

Proof. Let \(f(\theta)=a\cos m\theta\) and, for an integer \(j\), let \(I_j=\left[\frac{j\pi}m-\frac\pi{2m},\frac{j\pi}m+\frac\pi{2m}\right]\); these intervals have length \(\frac\pi m\) and cover \(\R\). The \(j\)-th arch is \(A_j=\{P(f(\theta),\theta):\theta\in I_j\}\). For \(\theta=\frac{j\pi}m+s\) with \(\abs s\le\frac\pi{2m}\) we have \(\cos m\theta=\cos(j\pi+ms)=(-1)^j\cos ms\), and \(\cos ms\ge0\), so \(f(\theta)=(-1)^ja\cos ms\): the sign of \(f\) on \(I_j\) is the constant sign of \((-1)^ja\), \(\abs f=\abs a\cos ms\) is \(0\) at the ends of \(I_j\) and equals \(\abs a\) at \(s=0\). Each arch is a petal. A point of \(A_j\) is on the ray at angle \(\theta=\frac{j\pi}m+s\) if \((-1)^ja>0\), and on the opposite ray if \((-1)^ja<0\). In both cases the point is on the ray at angle \(\varphi_j+s\), where \(\varphi_j=\frac{j\pi}m\) if \((-1)^ja>0\) and \(\varphi_j=\frac{j\pi}m+\pi\) otherwise, at distance \(\abs a\cos ms\). So \(A_j\) is the polar graph \(\rho=\abs a\cos ms\) over the sector of directions \(\varphi_j-\frac\pi{2m}\le\varphi\le\varphi_j+\frac\pi{2m}\): a simple closed loop through \(O\) with its tip at distance \(\abs a\) in the direction \(\varphi_j\). Two arches with the same \(\varphi_j\) (mod \(2\pi\)) are the same set; two arches with different \(\varphi_j\) (mod \(2\pi\)) lie in sectors of width \(\frac\pi m\) whose directions differ by a nonzero multiple of \(\frac\pi m\), so they meet only at \(O\). Counting. Take \(a>0\) (for \(a<0\) every \(\varphi_j\) is shifted by \(\pi\), which does not change the count). Then \(\varphi_j=\frac{n_j\pi}m\) with \(n_j=j\) for even \(j\) and \(n_j=j+m\) for odd \(j\), taken modulo \(2m\).

  • \(m\) even. Then \(n_j\equiv j\) modulo \(2\) for all \(j\). As \(j=0,1,\dots,2m-1\) runs through a full set of residues modulo \(2m\), so does \(n_j\): there are \(2m\) different directions and so \(2m\) petals. The arches \(A_0,\dots,A_{2m-1}\) fill the \(\theta\)-interval \(\left[-\frac\pi{2m},2\pi-\frac\pi{2m}\right]\) of length \(2\pi\), and \(f\) has period \(2\pi\).

  • \(m\) odd. Then \(n_j\) is even for all \(j\) (for odd \(j\), \(j+m\) is even), so there are at most \(m\) different directions. Moreover \(f(\theta+\pi)=a\cos(m\theta+m\pi)=-f(\theta)\), so \(P(f(\theta+\pi),\theta+\pi)=P(-f(\theta),\theta+\pi)=P(f(\theta),\theta)\) by Theorem 12.2.3: the curve repeats after \(\pi\). The arches \(A_0,\dots,A_{m-1}\) fill an interval of length \(\pi\), and their numbers are \(n_j=j\) for the even \(j\le m-1\) (that is \(\frac{m+1}2\) values) and \(n_j=j+m\in\{m+1,\dots,2m-1\}\) for the odd \(j\le m-1\) (\(\frac{m-1}2\) values): all different, so \(m\) petals.

Sine. \(\sin m\theta=\cos\left(m\theta-\frac\pi2\right)=\cos\bigl(m(\theta-\frac\pi{2m})\bigr)\), so \(P(r,\theta)\) is on the cosine rose exactly when \(P\left(r,\theta+\frac\pi{2m}\right)\) is on \(r=a\sin m\theta\): the second graph is the first rotated through \(\frac\pi{2m}\). ◻ ∎

Example 12.2.18: A three-petal rose

Graph \(r=4\cos3\theta\). Find the number of petals, the tips, the interval of \(\theta\) traced by each petal, and the tangent lines at the origin.

Solution. Here \(m=3\) is odd, so by Theorem 12.2.17 there are \(3\) petals and the whole curve is traced for \(0\le\theta\le\pi\). Zeros. \(\cos3\theta=0\) for \(3\theta=\frac\pi2+k\pi\), that is \(\theta=\frac\pi6+\frac{k\pi}3\): in \([0,\pi]\), \(\theta=\frac\pi6,\frac\pi2,\frac{5\pi}6\). Tips. \(\abs r=4\) when \(\cos3\theta=\pm1\), at \(\theta=0,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3\): \(r=4,-4,4\). The tip at \(\theta=0\) is \((4,0)\). The tip at \(\theta=\frac\pi3\) has \(r=-4\), so it is \(P\left(-4,\frac\pi3\right)=P\left(4,\frac{4\pi}3\right)=\left(4\cos\frac{4\pi}3,4\sin\frac{4\pi}3\right)=(-2,-2\sqrt3)\). The tip at \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}3\) is \(\left(4\cos\frac{2\pi}3,4\sin\frac{2\pi}3\right)=(-2,2\sqrt3)\). The three tips are \(4\) units from \(O\), in the directions \(0\), \(\frac{2\pi}3\), \(\frac{4\pi}3\), equally spaced. Petals and intervals. Between consecutive zeros \(f\) has constant sign: for \(-\frac\pi6\le\theta\le\frac\pi6\), \(r\ge0\): the petal around the \(x\)-axis (tip \((4,0)\)). For \(\frac\pi6\le\theta\le\frac\pi2\), \(r\le0\): the points are on the opposite rays, with angles between \(\frac{7\pi}6\) and \(\frac{3\pi}2\): the petal with tip \((-2,-2\sqrt3)\). For \(\frac\pi2\le\theta\le\frac{5\pi}6\), \(r\ge0\): the petal with tip \((-2,2\sqrt3)\). For \(\frac{5\pi}6\le\theta\le\frac{7\pi}6\), \(r\le0\) and the first petal is traced again (period \(\pi\)). Tangent lines at \(O\). \(f'(\theta)=-12\sin3\theta\), so \(f'\left(\frac\pi6\right)=-12\), \(f'\left(\frac\pi2\right)=12\), \(f'\left(\frac{5\pi}6\right)=-12\), all nonzero. By Theorem 12.2.13 the tangent lines at the origin are \(\theta=\frac\pi6\), \(\theta=\frac\pi2\) and \(\theta=\frac{5\pi}6\): the lines with slopes \(\frac1{\sqrt3}\), vertical, and \(-\frac1{\sqrt3}\). Each petal is bounded by two of these lines (Figure below).

Knowledge Check 12.2.3: Petals and periods

How many petals do \(r=3\sin7\theta\) and \(r=2\cos6\theta\) have, and over what interval of \(\theta\) is each traced once?

items.title: Lemniscates and spirals
items.text:
Example 12.2.19: A lemniscate

Graph \(r^2=4\cos2\theta\). Find the values of \(\theta\) for which the curve exists, the tips, the tangent lines at the origin, a Cartesian equation, and the symmetries.

Solution. Existence. \(r^2\ge0\), so \(\cos2\theta\ge0\): \(-\frac\pi4\le\theta\le\frac\pi4\) (and the same shifted by \(\pi\); no points exist for \(\frac\pi4<\theta<\frac{3\pi}4\)). For such \(\theta\), \(r=\pm2\sqrt{\cos2\theta}\). Two loops. The sign \(+\) gives the points \(P(2\sqrt{\cos2\theta},\theta)\), a loop in the directions \(-\frac\pi4\le\theta\le\frac\pi4\) (right of the origin). The sign \(-\) gives \(P(-2\sqrt{\cos2\theta},\theta)=P(2\sqrt{\cos2\theta},\theta+\pi)\), the mirror loop to the left. Tips. The largest \(\abs r\) is at \(\theta=0\): \(r=\pm2\), the points \((\pm2,0)\). At the origin. \(r=0\) at \(\theta=\pm\frac\pi4\); the curve is tangent there to the lines \(\theta=\pm\frac\pi4\), that is \(y=\pm x\). (Since \(r=2\sqrt{\cos2\theta}\) near these angles, Theorem 12.2.13 does not apply directly because \(f'\) is not finite there; the lines \(\theta=\pm\frac\pi4\) are nonetheless the directions in which \(r\to0\), so they are the directions in which the loops leave the origin.) Cartesian equation. Multiply by \(r^2\): \(r^4=4r^2\cos2\theta=4r^2\left(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta\right)=4\left(x^2-y^2\right)\), so

\[(x^2+y^2)^2=4\left(x^2-y^2\right).\]

The multiplication by \(r^2\) can add only the origin (Theorem 12.2.9(2)), and the origin is on the lemniscate, so the two graphs agree. Check. \(\theta=\frac\pi6\): \(r=\pm2\sqrt{\cos\frac\pi3}=\pm\sqrt2\); the point \(\left(\sqrt2\cos\frac\pi6,\sqrt2\sin\frac\pi6\right)=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)\approx(1.22,0.71)\) satisfies \((x^2+y^2)^2=\left(\frac64+\frac24\right)^2=4\) and \(4(x^2-y^2)=4\left(\frac64-\frac24\right)=4\). Symmetry. The equation \(r^2=4\cos2\theta\) is unchanged when \(r\) is replaced by \(-r\) (symmetry about the origin) and when \(\theta\) is replaced by \(-\theta\) (\(\cos\) is even: symmetry about the \(x\)-axis); hence also about the \(y\)-axis.

Answer. A figure eight with tips \((\pm2,0)\), tangent to \(y=\pm x\) at the origin, \((x^2+y^2)^2=4(x^2-y^2)\) (Figure below).

Example 12.2.20: Two spirals

(a) Describe the spiral of Archimedes \(r=\theta\), \(\theta\ge0\). (b) Describe \(r=\frac1\theta\) for \(\theta>0\), the hyperbolic spiral; show that it has a horizontal asymptote.

Solution. (a) By Theorem 12.2.13 the curve is \(x=\theta\cos\theta\), \(y=\theta\sin\theta\). The radial distance grows with \(\theta\) while the direction turns counterclockwise, so the curve spirals outward. Points: \(\theta=0\): \(O\); \(\theta=\frac\pi2\): \(\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)\); \(\theta=\pi\): \((-\pi,0)\); \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}2\): \(\left(0,-\frac{3\pi}2\right)\); \(\theta=2\pi\): \((2\pi,0)\). Successive crossings of the positive \(x\)-axis are at \(\theta=2\pi k\), \(r=2\pi k\), so the turns are always \(2\pi\) apart. (For \(\theta<0\) the point \(P(\theta,\theta)\) is \((\theta\cos\theta,\theta\sin\theta)\), which is the reflection of the point for \(-\theta\) in the \(y\)-axis: the other arm of the spiral.) (b) Here \(x=\frac{\cos\theta}\theta\), \(y=\frac{\sin\theta}\theta\). As \(\theta\to0^+\), \(r=\frac1\theta\to\infty\), \(x=\frac{\cos\theta}\theta\to+\infty\), while \(y=\frac{\sin\theta}\theta\to1\) by the basic limit of Calculus I. So the curve approaches the horizontal line \(y=1\) as it goes out to the right: the line \(y=1\) is a horizontal asymptote. As \(\theta\to\infty\), \(r\to0\) and the curve winds around the origin infinitely often without reaching it. Points: \(\theta=\frac\pi2\): \(\left(0,\frac2\pi\right)\); \(\theta=\pi\): \(\left(-\frac1\pi,0\right)\); \(\theta=2\pi\): \(\left(\frac1{2\pi},0\right)\).

items.title: Symmetry
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.21: Symmetry tests

Let \(\mathcal C\) be the graph of a polar equation \(E(r,\theta)=0\). If the equation is satisfied by \((r,\theta)\) whenever it is satisfied by one of the replacements below, then \(\mathcal C\) has the stated symmetry.

about the \(x\)-axis: \((r,-\theta)\) or \((-r,\pi-\theta)\) about the \(y\)-axis: \((r,\pi-\theta)\) or \((-r,-\theta)\) about the origin: \((-r,\theta)\) or \((r,\theta+\pi)\)

These tests are sufficient, not necessary: a curve can be symmetric although the particular replacement you try does not return the equation you started with.

Proof. Let \(P=(x,y)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\) be on \(\mathcal C\), with \((r,\theta)\) satisfying \(E=0\). \(x\)-axis. The reflection of \(P\) is \((x,-y)=(r\cos\theta,-r\sin\theta)\). Since \(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\) and \(\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\), this is \(P(r,-\theta)\). Also \((-r)\cos(\pi-\theta)=r\cos\theta\) and \((-r)\sin(\pi-\theta)=-r\sin\theta\), so it is \(P(-r,\pi-\theta)\). If the equation holds at \((r,-\theta)\) or at \((-r,\pi-\theta)\) whenever it holds at \((r,\theta)\), the reflection is on \(\mathcal C\). \(y\)-axis. The reflection is \((-x,y)=(-r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\). Since \(\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta\) and \(\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta\), it is \(P(r,\pi-\theta)\); since \((-r)\cos(-\theta)=-r\cos\theta\) and \((-r)\sin(-\theta)=r\sin\theta\), it is also \(P(-r,-\theta)\). Origin. The reflection is \((-x,-y)=(-r\cos\theta,-r\sin\theta)\), which is \(P(-r,\theta)\) and, since \(\cos(\theta+\pi)=-\cos\theta\) and \(\sin(\theta+\pi)=-\sin\theta\), also \(P(r,\theta+\pi)\). In each case the reflected point has a representation satisfying \(E=0\), so it is on \(\mathcal C\) (Definition 12.2.8). ◻ ∎

Example 12.2.22: Testing symmetry

Use Theorem 12.2.21 on \(r=\sin2\theta\).

Solution. \(x\)-axis. Replace \((r,\theta)\) by \((-r,\pi-\theta)\): the equation becomes \(-r=\sin(2\pi-2\theta)=-\sin2\theta\) (since \(\sin(2\pi-u)=-\sin u\)), which is equivalent to \(r=\sin2\theta\). So the curve is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis. (The first replacement, \((r,-\theta)\), gives \(r=-\sin2\theta\), which is not the original equation; this test fails, but the second succeeds.) \(y\)-axis. Replace by \((-r,-\theta)\): \(-r=\sin(-2\theta)=-\sin2\theta\), equivalent to the original. Symmetric about the \(y\)-axis. Origin. Replace by \((r,\theta+\pi)\): \(r=\sin(2\theta+2\pi)=\sin2\theta\), the original. Symmetric about the origin. This agrees with Theorem 12.2.17: \(r=\sin2\theta\) is a four-petal rose.

items.title: How far must \(\theta\) run?
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.23: Tracing the whole curve

Let \(f\) be defined for all \(\theta\) and \(P>0\).

  1. If \(f(\theta+P)=f(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\) and \(P\) is a multiple of \(2\pi\), the curve \(r=f(\theta)\) is traced completely on any \(\theta\)-interval of length \(P\) (\(P=2\pi\) is the smallest case).

  2. If \(f(\theta+P)=-f(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\) and \(P\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi\), the same is true.

  3. For \(r=\cos\frac{p\theta}q\) or \(r=\sin\frac{p\theta}q\) (\(p,q\) positive integers with no common factor), the whole curve is traced on any interval of length \(\pi q\) if \(p\) and \(q\) are both odd, and on any interval of length \(2\pi q\) otherwise.

Proof. (1) \(P(f(\theta+P),\theta+P)=P(f(\theta),\theta+P)=P(f(\theta),\theta)\) because \(P\) is a multiple of \(2\pi\) (Theorem 12.2.3). So the point for \(\theta+P\) is the point for \(\theta\); any \(\theta\) is congruent, by a multiple of \(P\), to a \(\theta\) in the given interval, and nothing new appears. (2) \(P(f(\theta+P),\theta+P)=P(-f(\theta),\theta+P)=P(-f(\theta),\theta+\pi)=P(f(\theta),\theta)\), using \(P-\pi\) a multiple of \(2\pi\) and then Theorem 12.2.3 twice (once to drop the multiple of \(2\pi\), once for the pair \((-r,\theta+\pi)\)). (3) Let \(f(\theta)=\cos\frac{p\theta}q\) (the sine case is identical). If \(p,q\) are odd, \(f(\theta+\pi q)=\cos\left(\frac{p\theta}q+p\pi\right)=-\cos\frac{p\theta}q=-f(\theta)\) because \(p\) is odd, and \(\pi q\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi\) because \(q\) is odd: case (2). Otherwise take \(P=2\pi q\): \(f(\theta+2\pi q)=\cos\left(\frac{p\theta}q+2\pi p\right)=f(\theta)\), a multiple of \(2\pi\): case (1). ◻ ∎

The theorem gives an interval that suffices; it does not claim that no shorter interval would do (for the rose \(r=\cos m\theta\) with \(m\) even the full \(2\pi\) is needed; Theorem 12.2.17).

Example 12.2.24: A curve that closes after two turns

Graph \(r=\cos\frac{3\theta}2\). Over what interval is it traced, and where is it for \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=2\pi\)?

Solution. Here \(p=3\), \(q=2\) have no common factor and \(q\) is even, so Theorem 12.2.23(3) gives the interval \(0\le\theta\le4\pi\). Check by hand: \(f(\theta+4\pi)=\cos\left(\frac{3\theta}2+6\pi\right)=f(\theta)\). After one turn the curve has not closed: \(f(\theta+2\pi)=\cos\left(\frac{3\theta}2+3\pi\right)=-f(\theta)\), and the point for \(\theta+2\pi\) is \(P(-f(\theta),\theta)\), the point of the opposite ray, which differs from \(P(f(\theta),\theta)\) whenever \(f(\theta)\ne0\). So the second turn draws a different part of the curve. Key points. \(\theta=0\): \(r=1\), the point \((1,0)\). \(\theta=2\pi\): \(r=\cos3\pi=-1\), the point \(P(-1,2\pi)=(-\cos2\pi,-\sin2\pi)=(-1,0)\). Zeros. \(\frac{3\theta}2=\frac\pi2+k\pi\) gives \(\theta=\frac\pi3,\pi,\frac{5\pi}3,\frac{7\pi}3,3\pi,\frac{11\pi}3\) in \([0,4\pi]\): six passes through the origin. Symmetry. \(f\) is even, so the curve is symmetric about the \(x\)-axis. The curve is the figure below.

items.title: Where two polar curves meet
items.text:
Finding intersections is where the non-uniqueness of polar coordinates does its damage. Solving \(f(\theta)=g(\theta)\) finds the points where both curves reach the same point at the same angle; it can miss points that the two curves reach with different representations.

Theorem 12.2.25: Intersections of polar curves

Let \(f\) and \(g\) have period \(2\pi\). A point \(P\ne O\) lies on both \(r=f(\theta)\) and \(r=g(\theta)\) if and only if there is a \(\theta\) with

\[\text{(A)}\ \ f(\theta)=g(\theta)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\text{(B)}\ \ f(\theta)=-g(\theta+\pi)\]

and \(P=P(f(\theta),\theta)\). The origin is on a curve if and only if its function has a zero; it is on both curves when each of \(f\) and \(g\) has a zero, which is not detected by (A) or (B) unless the zeros occur at related angles.

Proof. (\(\Leftarrow\)) Under (A), \(P(f(\theta),\theta)=P(g(\theta),\theta)\) is on both curves. Under (B), \(P(f(\theta),\theta)=P(-f(\theta),\theta+\pi)\) (Theorem 12.2.3) \(=P\bigl(g(\theta+\pi),\theta+\pi\bigr)\), which is on \(r=g(\theta)\) as well. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Let \(P\ne O\) be on both curves. Then \(P\) has a representation \((r_1,\theta_1)\) with \(r_1=f(\theta_1)\) and a representation \((r_2,\theta_2)\) with \(r_2=g(\theta_2)\). By Theorem 12.2.3, either \(r_2=r_1\) and \(\theta_2=\theta_1+2\pi k\), or \(r_2=-r_1\) and \(\theta_2=\theta_1+\pi+2\pi k\) (\(k\) an integer). In the first case \(g(\theta_1)=g(\theta_2)=r_2=r_1=f(\theta_1)\) by periodicity: (A) at \(\theta_1\). In the second case \(g(\theta_1+\pi)=g(\theta_2)=r_2=-r_1=-f(\theta_1)\): (B) at \(\theta_1\). The last sentence is the definition of the graph and the fact that \(r=0\) represents \(O\). ◻ ∎

Procedure 12.2.26: Intersections of \(r=f(\theta)\) and \(r=g(\theta)\)

  1. Solve (A) \(f(\theta)=g(\theta)\) and (B) \(f(\theta)=-g(\theta+\pi)\) for \(\theta\) in an interval of length \(2\pi\).

  2. Find the points \(P(f(\theta),\theta)\) for each solution; remove duplicates (compare Cartesian coordinates).

  3. Check the origin separately: solve \(f(\theta)=0\) and \(g(\theta)=0\).

  4. Draw both curves to confirm the count.

Example 12.2.27: Two cardioids: a hidden intersection

Find all intersections of \(r=1+\cos\theta\) and \(r=1-\cos\theta\).

Solution. \(f=1+\cos\theta\), \(g=1-\cos\theta\), both of period \(2\pi\). (A). \(1+\cos\theta=1-\cos\theta\) gives \(2\cos\theta=0\), so \(\theta=\frac\pi2\) or \(\frac{3\pi}2\), with \(r=1\): the points \((0,1)\) and \((0,-1)\). (B). \(g(\theta+\pi)=1-\cos(\theta+\pi)=1+\cos\theta\), so (B) reads \(1+\cos\theta=-(1+\cos\theta)\), that is \(\cos\theta=-1\), \(\theta=\pi\), \(r=f(\pi)=0\): the origin. Origin. \(f(\pi)=0\) and \(g(0)=0\): the origin is on both curves (reached at different angles, \(\pi\) and \(0\)). Equation (A) alone found only two points, and would have missed the origin. Answer. \((0,1)\), \((0,-1)\) and the origin.

Example 12.2.28: A rose and a circle: all eight points

Find all intersections of \(r=2\cos2\theta\) and \(r=1\).

Solution. \(g=1\) is constant, so \(g(\theta+\pi)=1\). (A). \(2\cos2\theta=1\), \(\cos2\theta=\frac12\), \(2\theta=\pm\frac\pi3+2\pi k\), so \(\theta=\pm\frac\pi6+\pi k\): in \([0,2\pi)\), \(\theta=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6,\frac{7\pi}6,\frac{11\pi}6\), each with \(r=1\). (B). \(2\cos2\theta=-1\), \(\cos2\theta=-\frac12\), \(2\theta=\pm\frac{2\pi}3+2\pi k\), so \(\theta=\pm\frac\pi3+\pi k\): \(\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{4\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}3\), each with \(r=f(\theta)=-1\); the points are \(P(-1,\theta)=P\left(1,\theta+\pi\right)\), on the unit circle at the angles \(\frac{4\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}3,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3\). Together the eight points are on the unit circle at the angles \(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}6,\frac{7\pi}6,\frac{4\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}3,\frac{11\pi}6\). A solution of (A) alone would give only four. Origin. The rose passes through \(O\) but the circle \(r=1\) does not, so \(O\) is not an intersection. Check with the picture: each of the four petals leaves the circle through two points.

items.title: Tangent lines to polar curves
items.text:
Theorem 12.2.29: Slope of a polar curve

Let \(r=f( heta)\) with \(f\) differentiable. At a point where \(x'( heta)=f'\cos heta-f\sin heta e0\), the slope of the tangent line is

\[ rac{dy}{dx}= rac{f'( heta)\sin heta+f( heta)\cos heta}{f'( heta)\cos heta-f( heta)\sin heta}.\]

The tangent is horizontal where the numerator is \(0\) and the denominator is not, and vertical where the denominator is \(0\) and the numerator is not.

Proof. By Theorem 12.2.13 the curve is parametric with \(x'=f'\cos heta-f\sin heta\) and \(y'=f'\sin heta+f\cos heta\). By the slope formula for parametric curves (Theorem 12.1.12), \( rac{dy}{dx}= rac{y'}{x'}\) wherever \(x' e0\). The statements on horizontal and vertical tangents are the same formula read at a zero of \(y'\) or \(x'\). ◻ ∎

Example 12.2.30: Tangent lines of a cardioid

Find the slope of the tangent line to \(r=1+\cos heta\) at \( heta= rac\pi3\) and at \( heta= rac\pi2\), and give the tangent lines.

Solution. \(f=1+\cos heta\), \(f'=-\sin heta\). Numerator. \(y'=f'\sin heta+f\cos heta=-\sin^2 heta+\cos heta+\cos^2 heta=\cos heta+\cos2 heta\), using \(\cos^2 heta-\sin^2 heta=\cos2 heta\). Denominator. \(x'=f'\cos heta-f\sin heta=-\sin heta\cos heta-\sin heta-\sin heta\cos heta=-\sin heta(1+2\cos heta)\). At \( heta= rac\pi3\). \(y'= rac12+\cos rac{2\pi}3= rac12- rac12=0\) and \(x'=- rac{\sqrt3}2\cdot2=-\sqrt3 e0\). The slope is \(0\): horizontal tangent. The point has \(r=1+ rac12= rac32\), so it is \(\left( rac32\cos rac\pi3, rac32\sin rac\pi3 ight)=\left( rac34, rac{3\sqrt3}4 ight)\) and the tangent line is \(y= rac{3\sqrt3}4\). At \( heta= rac\pi2\). \(y'=0+\cos\pi=-1\) and \(x'=-1\cdot(1+0)=-1\). The slope is \( rac{-1}{-1}=1\). The point has \(r=1\), so it is \((0,1)\), and the tangent line is \(y-1=x\), that is \(y=x+1\). Check. From \(r=1+\cos heta\) we get \(r^2=r+x\), so \(r=r^2-x\) and, squaring the relation \(r=r^2-x\), the Cartesian equation \((x^2+y^2-x)^2=x^2+y^2\). The point \((0,1)\) gives \((1-0)^2=1\), and \(\left( rac34, rac{3\sqrt3}4 ight)\) has \(x^2+y^2= rac9{16}+ rac{27}{16}= rac94\), so \(\left( rac94- rac34 ight)^2=\left( rac32 ight)^2= rac94\).

Pause and think 12.2.3: Why (B) did not matter

In Example 12.2.28, equation (B) produced four points that (A) missed. Now take the three-petal rose \(r=\cos3 heta\) and the circle \(r= rac12\). Show that every solution of (B) gives a point that is already found by (A) at the angle \( heta+\pi\). (Hint: compare \(f( heta+\pi)\) with \(f( heta)\).)

Answer and discussion

For \(f( heta)=\cos3 heta\) we have \(f( heta+\pi)=\cos(3 heta+3\pi)=-\cos3 heta=-f( heta)\). A solution of (B), \(f( heta)=- rac12\), therefore satisfies \(f( heta+\pi)=-f( heta)= rac12=g( heta+\pi)\): so \( heta+\pi\) solves (A), and the point \(P\left(f( heta+\pi), heta+\pi ight)\) found by (A) is \(P\left( rac12, heta+\pi ight)=P\left(- rac12, heta ight)=P(f( heta), heta)\), the point that (B) produced. The same argument works for every \(f\) with \(f( heta+\pi)=-f( heta)\), which is the case for roses with an odd number of petals; for the rose with an even number \(f( heta+\pi)=f( heta)\) and (B) really is new.

items.title: Looking ahead
items.text: A polar equation is a recipe for a parametric curve, so the tools of Section 12.1 apply: Theorem 12.2.13 says that the speed of a polar curve is \(\sqrt{f^2+f'^2}\), which is exactly what an arc length integral needs, and the sectors of angle \(d\theta\) that sweep out a rose petal suggest how to compute areas. Both are the subject of Section 12.3 (area and arc length in polar coordinates). In Section 12.4 the circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas reappear as conic sections, and a single polar equation, \(r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}\), will describe all of them. In a later chapter, polar coordinates in the plane are extended to cylindrical coordinates in space by adding a height, and to spherical coordinates by tilting the ray out of the plane; the conversion formulas of Theorem 12.2.2 carry over almost word for word.

items.title: Example bank
items.text:
What’s in this bank. Twenty further worked examples, grouped by problem type and ordered from easiest to hardest within each group.

  1. Points and conversions (Examples 12.2.31–12.2.33): a negative radial coordinate; Cartesian to polar in the second quadrant; a distance.

  2. Equations, lines and circles (Examples 12.2.34–12.2.36): a circle from its polar equation; a line in polar form; a circle with a center away from the axes.

  3. Graphing (Examples 12.2.37–12.2.39): a cardioid; a five-petal rose; a logarithmic spiral.

  4. Symmetry and period (Examples 12.2.40–12.2.41): a lemniscate whose symmetry tests mostly fail; periods of two curves.

  5. Tangent lines (Examples 12.2.42–12.2.44): a spiral; horizontal and vertical tangents of a cardioid; a rose.

  6. Intersections (Examples 12.2.45–12.2.47): two circles; a circle and a cardioid meeting at the origin; a lemniscate and a circle.

  7. Proofs (Examples 12.2.48–12.2.50).

items.title: Group 1: Points and conversions
items.text:
Example 12.2.31: A negative radial coordinate

Convert \(\left(-3,-\frac{5\pi}6\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates, and give its representation with \(r>0\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

Solution. \(x=-3\cos\left(-\frac{5\pi}6\right)=-3\cdot\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=\frac{3\sqrt3}2\) and \(y=-3\sin\left(-\frac{5\pi}6\right)=-3\cdot\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac32\), using \(\cos(-u)=\cos u\), \(\sin(-u)=-\sin u\), \(\cos\frac{5\pi}6=-\frac{\sqrt3}2\), \(\sin\frac{5\pi}6=\frac12\). The point is \(\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}2,\frac32\right)\). Its distance from \(O\) is \(\sqrt{\frac{27}4+\frac94}=\sqrt9=3\) and its angle satisfies \(\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}2\), \(\sin\theta=\frac12\), so \(\theta=\frac\pi6\). Answer. \(\left(3,\frac\pi6\right)\). Check by Theorem 12.2.3: \(\left(-3,-\frac{5\pi}6\right)=\left(3,-\frac{5\pi}6+\pi\right)=\left(3,\frac\pi6\right)\).

Example 12.2.32: Cartesian to polar in the second quadrant

Give two polar representations of \((-2,2\sqrt3)\): one with \(r>0\) and one with \(r<0\), both with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\).

Solution. \(r=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(2\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{4+12}=4\).
