Then \( rac fg=f\cdot rac1g=\sum q_n(x-a)^n\) on \(\abs{x-a}<\min( ho_1,R)=: ho\) by Theorem H.2, where \(q_n=\sum_{j=0}^na_jr_{n-j}\). Apply Theorem H.2 again to \(g\) and \(\sum q_n(x-a)^n\): for \(\abs{x-a}< ho\),

\[f(x)=g(x)\cdot rac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^nb_jq_{n-j}\Bigr)(x-a)^n .\]

Both sides are power series in \((x-a)\) equal on an interval, so their coefficients agree (by Theorem F.6, the coefficient of \((x-a)^n\) in a power series is \( rac{1}{n!}\) times the \(n\)-th derivative of its sum at \(a\)). Hence \(a_n=\sum_{j=0}^nb_jq_{n-j}\); solving for \(q_n\) (the term \(j=0\) is \(b_0q_n\)) gives the formula. ◻ ∎

Example H.5: The product \(e^x\cdot rac1{1-x}\)

Find the first terms of the Maclaurin series of \(\dfrac{e^x}{1-x}\), and the limit of its coefficients.

Solution. With \(a_j= rac1{j!}\) (valid for all \(x\)) and \(b_k=1\) (valid for \(\abs x<1\)), Theorem H.2 with \(R=1\) gives \(c_n=\sum_{j=0}^n rac1{j!}\cdot1\), the partial sums of the series for \(e\):

\[ rac{e^x}{1-x}=1+2x+ rac52x^2+ rac83x^3+ rac{65}{24}x^4+ rac{163}{60}x^5+\cdots\qquad(\abs x<1).\]

The coefficients increase to \(e=2.71828\dots\), because \(c_n=\sum_{j\le n} rac1{j!} o e\).

Example H.6: The first terms of \( an x\)

Use Theorem H.4 with \(f=\sin x\) and \(g=\cos x\) to find the first four nonzero terms of the series of \( an x\).

Solution. \(f\) has \(a_1=1\), \(a_3=- rac16\), \(a_5= rac1{120}\), \(a_7=- rac1{5040}\) and zero for the other indices up to \(7\); \(g\) has \(b_0=1\), \(b_2=- rac12\), \(b_4= rac1{24}\), \(b_6=- rac1{720}\) and zero for odd indices. By the formula \(q_n=a_n-\sum_{j=1}^nb_jq_{n-j}\) (here \(b_0=1\)): \(q_0=0\); \(q_1=a_1=1\); \(q_2=-b_2q_0=0\); \(q_3=a_3-b_2q_1=- rac16+ rac12= rac13\); \(q_4=0\); \(q_5=a_5-b_2q_3-b_4q_1= rac1{120}+ rac16- rac1{24}= rac2{15}\); \(q_7=a_7-b_2q_5-b_4q_3-b_6q_1=- rac1{5040}+ rac1{15}- rac1{72}+ rac1{720}= rac{17}{315}\). So

\[ an x=x+ rac{x^3}3+ rac{2x^5}{15}+ rac{17x^7}{315}+\cdots\]

on some interval about \(0\) (Theorem H.4 guarantees one; its length is not found by this method).

items.title: Appendix I. Parametrizations and Arc Length
items.text:
Section 12.1 computes the length of a curve, the area under it and the area of the surface it generates from a parametrization, and a curve has many parametrizations. Why does the answer not depend on the one we choose? This section proves it, for curves that are traced once. Three things are shown: two such parametrizations of the same set of points are related by a monotone change of parameter (Theorem I.3); the arc length is therefore the same (Theorem I.4); and when the change of parameter is differentiable, the integrals for arc length, surface area and area are unchanged by the substitution rule (Theorem I.5). The facts used from Section 12.1, stated in words only, are: if \(\gamma(t)=(f(t),g(t))\), \(a\le t\le b\), has continuous \(f',g'\), then the length of the inscribed polygon for a partition \(\Pi\) satisfies \(\ell(\Pi)\le L=\int_a^b\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt\), and \(\ell(\Pi)\to L\) as the mesh of \(\Pi\) tends to \(0\).

A parametrization \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) is a simple arc if it is continuous and one-to-one. (A closed curve traced once, such as a circle, returns to its start; it is handled by cutting it at one point into two simple arcs, and lengths add.)

Theorem I.1: Bolzano–Weierstrass

Every sequence \(\{s_n\}\) in a closed interval \([a,b]\) has a convergent subsequence, with limit in \([a,b]\).

Proof. Call an index \(m\) a peak if \(s_m\ge s_n\) for all \(n>m\). If there are infinitely many peaks \(m_1<m_2<\cdots\), then \(s_{m_1}\ge s_{m_2}\ge\cdots\) is a nonincreasing subsequence. If there are finitely many, let \(n_1\) be larger than all of them. Then \(n_1\) is not a peak, so there is \(n_2>n_1\) with \(s_{n_2}>s_{n_1}\); \(n_2\) is not a peak either, so there is \(n_3>n_2\) with \(s_{n_3}>s_{n_2}\), and so on: an increasing subsequence. In both cases we have a monotone subsequence bounded by \(a\) and \(b\), which converges by the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem A.5); its limit is in \([a,b]\) because the limit respects bounds (Theorem A.6). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.2: The inverse of a simple arc is continuous

Let \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) be continuous and one-to-one, with image \(C\). Then the inverse \(\gamma^{-1}:C\to[a,b]\) is continuous: if \(\gamma(s_n)\to\gamma(s)\) then \(s_n\to s\).

Proof. Suppose \(\gamma(s_n)\to\gamma(s)\) but \(s_n\not\to s\). Then there is \(\varepsilon>0\) and a subsequence with \(\abs{s_{n_j}-s}\ge\varepsilon\) for all \(j\). By Theorem I.1 a further subsequence converges to some \(s'\in[a,b]\), and \(\abs{s'-s}\ge\varepsilon\). By continuity of \(\gamma\), \(\gamma(s_{n_{j_i}})\to\gamma(s')\) (limits of points of the plane are taken coordinatewise). But this subsequence also tends to \(\gamma(s)\), so \(\gamma(s')=\gamma(s)\) by uniqueness of limits (Theorem B.1), and \(s'=s\) because \(\gamma\) is one-to-one. This contradicts \(\abs{s'-s}\ge\varepsilon\). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.3: Two simple arcs with the same image

Let \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\R^2\) and \(\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to\R^2\) be simple arcs with the same image \(C\). Then \(\varphi=\gamma^{-1}\circ\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to[a,b]\) is a continuous, strictly monotone bijection and \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\).

Proof. \(\varphi\) is a bijection because \(\tilde\gamma:[c,d]\to C\) and \(\gamma^{-1}:C\to[a,b]\) are, and it is continuous by Theorem I.2 (if \(s_n\to s\) then \(\tilde\gamma(s_n)\to\tilde\gamma(s)\), hence \(\varphi(s_n)\to\varphi(s)\)). Clearly \(\gamma\circ\varphi=\tilde\gamma\). A continuous one-to-one function on an interval is strictly monotone. To see this, first note that for \(s_1<s_2<s_3\) the value \(\varphi(s_2)\) lies strictly between \(\varphi(s_1)\) and \(\varphi(s_3)\): otherwise, say \(\varphi(s_2)\) is larger than both, choose \(w\) with \(\max(\varphi(s_1),\varphi(s_3))<w<\varphi(s_2)\); the Intermediate Value Theorem gives \(u\in(s_1,s_2)\) and \(u'\in(s_2,s_3)\) with \(\varphi(u)=w=\varphi(u')\), contradicting one-to-one (the case “smaller than both” is the same). Now suppose \(\varphi(c)<\varphi(d)\) (the other case is symmetric). For \(c<s<s'\le d\) we have \(\varphi(c)<\varphi(s)\) by the statement for \(c<s<d\) (or \(s'\)), and \(\varphi(s)\) lies between \(\varphi(c)\) and \(\varphi(s')\), which forces \(\varphi(s)<\varphi(s')\). So \(\varphi\) is strictly increasing. ◻ ∎

Theorem I.4: Arc length does not depend on the parametrization

Let \(\gamma\) and \(\tilde\gamma\) be simple arcs with the same image \(C\) and continuous derivatives. Then they give the same length: \(\int_a^b\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt=\int_c^d\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}\,ds\). This common value is the supremum of the lengths of all polygons inscribed in \(C\) with vertices in order along \(C\).

Proof. By the facts quoted at the start, \(\ell(\Pi)\le L\) for every partition and \(\ell(\Pi)\to L\) as the mesh tends to \(0\), so \(L=\sup\ell(\Pi)\) (the supremum over all partitions of \([a,b]\)), and the same holds for \(\tilde L\) with partitions of \([c,d]\). Let \(\varphi\) be as in Theorem I.3. A partition \(s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_n\) of \([c,d]\) is carried by the strictly monotone bijection \(\varphi\) to the points \(t_k=\varphi(s_k)\), which, taken in increasing order (this reverses the order if \(\varphi\) is decreasing), form a partition of \([a,b]\), and \(\gamma(t_k)=\tilde\gamma(s_k)\): the two inscribed polygons have the same vertices and the same length. Every partition of \([a,b]\) arises this way, because \(\varphi\) is onto. So the two sets of polygon lengths are equal, hence so are the suprema, \(L=\tilde L\). ◻ ∎

Theorem I.5: Differentiable changes of parameter

Let \(\gamma=(f,g)\) be defined on \([a,b]\) with \(f',g'\) continuous, and let \(\varphi:[c,d]\to[a,b]\) have a continuous derivative that is nonnegative throughout or nonpositive throughout, with \(\varphi\) onto. Put \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\). For every continuous function \(h\) on \([a,b]\),

\[\int_c^dh(\varphi(s))\,\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}\,ds=\int_a^bh(t)\,\abs{\gamma'(t)}\,dt,\qquad \int_c^dh(\varphi(s))\,\abs{(f\circ\varphi)'(s)}\,ds=\int_a^bh(t)\,\abs{f'(t)}\,dt.\]

In particular the arc length (\(h=1\)), the surface area of revolution (\(h=2\pi g\) or \(2\pi f\)) and the area under a curve (\(h=g\), with \(\abs{f'}\)) are the same for \(\tilde\gamma\) as for \(\gamma\).

Proof. By the Chain Rule \(\tilde\gamma'(s)=\gamma'(\varphi(s))\,\varphi'(s)\), so \(\abs{\tilde\gamma'(s)}=\abs{\gamma'(\varphi(s))}\,\abs{\varphi'(s)}\), and likewise \(\abs{(f\circ\varphi)'(s)}=\abs{f'(\varphi(s))}\,\abs{\varphi'(s)}\). Put \(H(t)=h(t)\abs{\gamma'(t)}\) (or \(h(t)\abs{f'(t)}\)), a continuous function. If \(\varphi'\ge0\), then \(\varphi\) is nondecreasing and onto, so \(\varphi(c)=a\), \(\varphi(d)=b\), and the substitution rule gives \(\int_c^dH(\varphi(s))\varphi'(s)\,ds=\int_a^bH(t)\,dt\), which is the claim because \(\abs{\varphi'}=\varphi'\). If \(\varphi'\le0\), then \(\varphi(c)=b\), \(\varphi(d)=a\), \(\abs{\varphi'}=-\varphi'\), and the substitution rule gives \(\int_c^dH(\varphi(s))(-\varphi'(s))\,ds=-\int_b^aH(t)\,dt=\int_a^bH(t)\,dt\). ◻ ∎

The hypothesis “traced once” cannot be dropped: the formulas measure what is traced, with multiplicity.

Example I.6: The half circle in two ways

The half circle is parametrized by \(\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\), \(0\le t\le\pi\), and by \(\tilde\gamma(s)=(\cos s^2,\sin s^2)\), \(0\le s\le\sqrt\pi\), that is, \(\tilde\gamma=\gamma\circ\varphi\) with \(\varphi(s)=s^2\), \(\varphi'(s)=2s\ge0\). The speed of \(\gamma\) is \(1\) and the speed of \(\tilde\gamma\) is \(2s\), so

\[\int_0^\pi1\,dt=\pi=\int_0^{\sqrt\pi}2s\,ds,\]

as Theorem I.4 predicts. If instead the circle is run twice, \(0\le t\le4\pi\), the formula gives \(4\pi\): that parametrization is not one-to-one, and the theorem does not apply.
